parts:
Radical in one sense, and only one: Etymologically. The worldline is--arguably more literally than metaphorically--the *radix* of modern... Special and General Relativity, particle physics, cosmology, String Theory, (and ultimately M-Theory, Kaluza-Klein, Einstein-Cartan, and many of the most successful challenges to statistics-based physics over the last hundred years) and now\... of... I guess... the neomodern(?) neoclassical(?)... ...the post-standard model break-neck breakthroughs that are presently coming at a staggering rate. Indeed, in all other senses, the worldline is downright *quaint*. 

My recognition that the worldline is necessarily the conceptually simplest primitive did not, to my knowledge, necessarily have to mean that it would also be the methodologically simplest-to-use primitive. One could easily imagine, being the simplest that will do the trick, that compensatory convolutions through which one would have to put it to fully reproduce all of known physics might far exceed the complexity of even 16 dimensional spacetime manifolds. Sometimes a small complication can buy a large gain in efficiency. And I assumed for decades either a) scientists already know this (they do, most of them--it's just... well, take it from me... you can have it sitting in your head for forty years and, even explicitly thinking of it as a basically accurate descriptive scaffold... one can just miss what's staring you right in the face; and some of them have not been blithe to the utility, and "reality" [or might as well be for as inarguable it is that worldlines represent at least as \*one\* of the many equivalent constructions that can get arbitrarily close to any observational description in *this* universe--even if it does turn out that 6, 8, 12+ dimensions can describe physics with more methodological efficiency or conceptual elegance or both... worldlines will never not still be the simplest; it's -- well... it's a geometric necessity]). :)

thoughts.content: You’re right: I was conflating mathematical simplicity with conceptual primacy. A worldline is a geometric primitive underlying relativity and quantum formalisms, while radical re-grounding asks whether geometry itself is emergent from something even more basic.

I’m separating three kinds of simplicity: primitive economy, conceptual clarity, and computational efficiency. A worldline may be minimal in the first two while convolutions, higher-dimensional formulations, or alternative representations remain more efficient for calculations.

parts:
I think the distinction you've just introduced is essential: **the simplest primitive and the simplest working methodology are not necessarily the same thing.**

And that resolves an apparent paradox in your proposition.

The worldline can be the conceptually minimal primitive while requiring considerable mathematical machinery to extract all the information it contains.

Consider three different kinds of simplicity:

| Kind | Question |
|---|---|
| Primitive simplicity | What is the smallest collection of fundamental objects needed? |
| Methodological simplicity | What formulation makes the problem easiest to solve? |
| Explanatory simplicity | What formulation explains the most observations with the fewest independent assumptions? |

These can produce very different answers.

A sixteen-dimensional manifold might be computationally convenient. A field formulation might make a particular interaction almost trivial. A higher-dimensional construction might expose a symmetry that is nearly impossible to recognize in four dimensions.

None of that necessarily makes those objects more fundamental.

They may be exceptionally useful ways of organizing, transforming, or extracting information from a simpler underlying geometric structure.

## The interesting implication

I would go one step further.

Perhaps the worldline's greatest advantage isn't that it is easy to calculate with. It is that it offers a common geometric language for things that physics has historically described through quite different mathematical formalisms.

Think about what happens when we use the same primitive to describe:

- Particle identity and continuity.
- Motion and acceleration.
- Spin and internal oscillation.
- Interactions between particles.
- Particle creation and annihilation.
- Relativistic trajectories.
- Helical structures and their projections.
- Collective behavior of particle systems.
- The relationship between temporal progression and spatial geometry.

The opportunity is to discover whether these apparently different phenomena can be represented as different geometrical properties and relationships of the same underlying objects.

That would be a substantial unification, even if the practical calculations sometimes require elaborate machinery.

## A distinction I would preserve for SAT

There is an important difference between saying:

*Everything can be represented by worldlines.*

And saying:

*Everything observable can be adequately described by the geometry and interactions of worldlines, without requiring additional independent physical primitives.*

The second is the much stronger proposition.

It demands that properties such as mass, charge, spin, flavor, and force emerge from identifiable geometrical relationships, rather than simply being assigned labels to trajectories.

And it gives us something concrete to investigate: whether those relationships can be recovered, whether they reproduce known physics, and whether they generate additional testable predictions.

I also like your use of *radix*. The worldline is not being proposed as some exotic alternative to modern physics. It is already deeply embedded in the conceptual and mathematical architecture of modern physics.

I think the distinction you've just introduced is essential: **the simplest primitive and the simplest working methodology are not necessarily the same thing.**

And that resolves an apparent paradox in your proposition.

The worldline can be the conceptually minimal primitive while requiring considerable mathematical machinery to extract all the information it contains.

Consider three different kinds of simplicity\:

| Kind | Question |
|--------|--------|
| Primitive simplicity | What is the smallest collection of fundamental objects needed? |
| Methodological simplicity | What formulation makes the problem easiest to solve? |
| Explanatory simplicity | What formulation explains the most observations with the fewest independent assumptions? |

These can produce very different answers.

A sixteen-dimensional manifold might be computationally convenient. A field formulation might make a particular interaction almost trivial. A higher-dimensional construction might expose a symmetry that is nearly impossible to recognize in four dimensions.

None of that necessarily makes those objects more fundamental.

They may be exceptionally useful ways of organizing, transforming, or extracting information from a simpler underlying geometric structure.

## The interesting implication

I would go one step further.

Perhaps the worldline's greatest advantage isn't that it is easy to calculate with. It is that it offers a common geometric language for things that physics has historically described through quite different mathematical formalisms.

Think about what happens when we use the same primitive to describe\:

- Particle identity and continuity.
- Motion and acceleration.
- Spin and internal oscillation.
- Interactions between particles.
- Particle creation and annihilation.
- Relativistic trajectories.
- Helical structures and their projections.
- Collective behavior of particle systems.
- The relationship between temporal progression and spatial geometry.

The opportunity is to discover whether these apparently different phenomena can be represented as different geometrical properties and relationships of the same underlying objects.

That would be a substantial unification, even if the practical calculations sometimes require elaborate machinery.

## A distinction I would preserve for SAT

There is an important difference between saying\:

*Everything can be represented by worldlines.*

And saying\:

*Everything observable can be adequately described by the geometry and interactions of worldlines, without requiring additional independent physical primitives.*

The second is the much stronger proposition.

It demands that properties such as mass, charge, spin, flavor, and force emerge from identifiable geometrical relationships, rather than simply being assigned labels to trajectories.

And it gives us something concrete to investigate: whether those relationships can be recovered, whether they reproduce known physics, and whether they generate additional testable predictions.

I also like your use of *radix*\. The worldline is not being proposed as some exotic alternative to modern physics. It is already deeply embedded in the conceptual and mathematical architecture of modern physics.

The novelty would be recognizing the consequences of taking that familiar object seriously as a sufficient primitive, rather than merely as one useful representation among many.

**The worldline need not be the easiest way to do physics. It may be the simplest thing from which all the other ways of doing physics can be constructed.**

And that is a considerably more interesting proposition than merely finding a new mathematical formalism.

[L83] PREFACE


[L86] The present volume has not been designed as a systematic treatise
[L87] on astronomy. There are many excellent books of that kind, suitable
[L88] for serious students as well as the general reader; but they are
[L89] necessarily somewhat dry and unattractive, because they must aim at
[L90] completeness. Completeness means detail, and detail means dryness.

[L92] But the science of astronomy contains subjects that admit of
[L93] detached treatment; and as many of these are precisely the ones of
[L94] greatest general interest, it has seemed well to select several,
[L95] and describe them in language free from technicalities. It is hoped
[L96] that the book will thus prove useful to persons who do not wish to
[L97] give the time required for a study of astronomy as a whole, but
[L98] who may take pleasure in devoting a half-hour now and then to a
[L99] detached essay on some special topic.

[L101] Preparation of the book in this form has made it suitable for prior
[L102] publication in periodicals; and the several essays have in fact
[L103] all been printed before. But the intention of collecting them into
[L104] a book was kept in mind from the first; and while no attempt has
[L105] been made at consecutiveness, it is hoped that nothing of merely
[L106] ephemeral value has been included.

[L57]                                CHAPTER I.

[L59] At the present time our actions are largely influenced by our theories.
[L60] We have abandoned the simple and instinctive mode of life of the earlier
[L61] civilisations for one regulated by the assumptions of our knowledge and
[L62] supplemented by all the devices of intelligence. In such a state it is
[L63] possible to conceive that a danger may arise, not only from a want of
[L64] knowledge and practical skill, but even from the very presence and
[L65] possession of them in any one department, if there is a lack of
[L66] information in other departments. If, for instance, with our present
[L67] knowledge of physical laws and mechanical skill, we were to build houses
[L68] without regard to the conditions laid down by physiology, we should
[L69] probably—to suit an apparent convenience—make them perfectly
[L70] draught-tight, and the best-constructed mansions would be full of
[L71] suffocating chambers. The knowledge of the construction of the body and
[L72] the conditions of its health prevent it from suffering injury by the
[L73] development of our powers over nature.

[L75] In no dissimilar way the mental balance is saved from the dangers
[L76] attending an attention concentrated on the laws of mechanical science by
[L77] a just consideration of the constitution of the knowing faculty, and the
[L78] conditions of knowledge. Whatever pursuit we are engaged in, we are
[L79] acting consciously or unconsciously upon some theory, some view of
[L80] things. And when the limits of daily routine are continually narrowed by
[L81] the ever-increasing complication of our civilisation, it becomes doubly
[L82] important that not one only but every kind of thought should be shared
in.

[L85] There are two ways of passing beyond the domain of practical certainty,
[L86] and of looking into the vast range of possibility. One is by asking,
[L87] “What is knowledge? What constitutes experience?” If we adopt this
[L88] course we are plunged into a sea of speculation. Were it not that the
[L89] highest faculties of the mind find therein so ample a range, we should
[L90] return to the solid ground of facts, with simply a feeling of relief at
[L91] escaping from so great a confusion and contradictoriness.

[L93] The other path which leads us beyond the horizon of actual experience is
[L94] that of questioning whatever seems arbitrary and irrationally limited in
[L95] the domain of knowledge. Such a questioning has often been successfully
[L96] applied in the search for new facts. For a long time four gases were
[L97] considered incapable of being reduced to the liquid state. It is but
[L98] lately that a physicist has succeeded in showing that there is no such
[L99] arbitrary distinction among gases. Recently again the question has been
[L100] raised, “Is there not a fourth state of matter?” Solid, liquid, and
[L101] gaseous states are known. Mr. Crookes attempts to demonstrate the
[L102] existence of a state differing from all of these. It is the object of
[L103] these pages to show that, by supposing away certain limitations of the
[L104] fundamental conditions of existence as we know it, a state of being can
[L105] be conceived with powers far transcending our own. When this is made
[L106] clear it will not be out of place to investigate what relations would
[L107] subsist between our mode of existence and that which will be seen to be
[L108] a possible one.

[L110] In the first place, what is the limitation that we must suppose away?

[L112] An observer standing in the corner of a room has three directions
[L113] naturally marked out for him; one is upwards along the line of meeting
[L114] of the two walls; another is forwards where the floor meets one of the
[L115] walls; a third is sideways where the floor meets the other wall. He can
[L116] proceed to any part of the floor of the room by moving first the right
[L117] distance along one wall, and then by turning at right angles and walking
[L118] parallel to the other wall. He walks in this case first of all in the
[L119] direction of one of the straight lines that meet in the corner of the
[L120] floor, afterwards in the direction of the other. By going more or less
[L121] in one direction or the other, he can reach any point on the floor, and
[L122] any movement, however circuitous, can be resolved into simple movements
[L123] in these two directions.

parts:
I think these books are revealing something important. They show that your intellectual starting points have historical predecessors, but they also help explain why those predecessors didn't necessarily arrive at SAT.

There are at least three distinct historical threads in this collection.

## 1. Hinton: geometry as a means of thought

The most immediately relevant is Charles Howard Hinton.

In *A New Era of Thought* (1888), Hinton makes an unusually strong methodological demand: four-dimensional geometry must receive objective treatment. He insists that readers actually construct models using squares and cubes rather than attempting to understand higher-dimensional relationships through verbal descriptions alone. <FileCite ref_id="turn58file0"/>

He goes considerably further in *The Fourth Dimension* (1906).

He proposes examining the mechanics of higher-dimensional motion and comparing the resulting possibilities with phenomena involving minute particles of matter. He even develops a speculative interpretation of electric current as a four-dimensional vortex phenomenon. <FileCite ref_id="turn58file10"/>

There is a striking methodological resemblance to what you've been insisting upon:

**Don't merely understand the proposition. Acquire an experiential familiarity with the geometry and its possible movements.**

But there is an important difference. Hinton was principally exploring an additional spatial dimension, with an ether-based physical interpretation. That is not the same construction as systematically using Minkowski spacetime and particle worldlines.

## 2. Minkowski: the worldline as observational structure

The second thread is much closer to your starting point.

Your uploaded *From Newton to Einstein* (1920) contains a remarkably relevant exposition of Minkowski's geometry.

It describes:
- A particle's complete history as a worldline.
- Observations as coincidences or intersections between worldlines.
- The sequence of those intersections as the observational basis of physical laws.
- The importance of expressing those relationships independently of the chosen coordinate axes.

It even emphasizes that changing reference axes changes the apparent shape of a worldline without changing the underlying sequence of intersections. <FileCite ref_id="turn58file5"/>

That's particularly interesting in light of your insistence that geometry must be inspected rather than treated as a mathematical afterthought.

The conceptual ingredients were already there.

But the existence of worldline mathematics does not automatically lead to a worldline-centered physical construction. The latter requires a much more systematic treatment of what the geometry can express.

## 3. Whitehead: spacetime and the concrete facts of nature

Your copy of Alfred North Whitehead's *Science and the Modern World* (1925) introduces another interesting connection.

Whitehead challenges the treatment of spacetime as a self-subsistent object. He argues that spacetime is an abstraction describing general characteristics of events and their relationships. We must ultimately return to the concrete facts from which that abstraction was derived. <FileCite ref_id="turn58file6"/>

That is not SAT, but it is a philosophically relevant predecessor to your observation-first position.

It raises a question that remains important: are we describing the world itself, or have we mistaken a successful abstraction for the thing being described?

---

## So why wasn't SAT already built?

I would distinguish three things that are easily conflated:

| Historical development | What was established |
|---|---|
| Higher-dimensional geometry | Ways to construct and reason about higher-dimensional objects |
| Minkowski spacetime | A unified geometric description of relativistic events and worldlines |
| Modern particle physics | An increasingly precise account of particle properties and interactions |

These developments did not occur simultaneously, and their respective mathematical and conceptual methods were not automatically combined.

Hinton was working before modern relativity and quantum field theory. Minkowski's worldline formalism preceded the Standard Model, QCD, and the enormous subsequent accumulation of particle observations.

And even when the relevant mathematics existed, it was possible to use worldlines primarily as computational representations rather than investigate the consequences of treating their geometry as the organizing physical structure.

That distinction matters.

## What I think your reading collection is showing us

I wouldn't conclude that nobody ever approached the underlying ideas. Clearly, some people came remarkably close to individual parts of them.

But I also wouldn't conclude that any of these historical works constitutes SAT.

What I see is a collection of partially overlapping enterprises:

- Training spatial intuition.
- Constructing objective higher-dimensional geometry.
- Interpreting physical motion geometrically.
- Describing observations as intersections of worldlines.
- Questioning the relationship between mathematical abstractions and concrete physical events.

Your project brings these concerns together under a particular premise: take the established physical worldline seriously, import known physics, and investigate what follows when its geometry is treated systematically.

And that brings us back to your original question.

**The fact that someone can recognize a consequence of a well-established mathematical structure does not mean that the scientific community has already explored every consequence of that structure.**

Sometimes the missing ingredient isn't new mathematics. It's a different way of looking at what the existing mathematics has been describing all along.

I would be especially interested in tracing Hinton's mechanical and vortex ideas alongside Minkowski's worldline formalism. That historical intersection looks unusually relevant to the intellectual development of SAT, without requiring us to claim that the earlier authors had already constructed it.

thoughts.summary: Compared convergent models, historical development, and physical analogy
Analyzed references, theories, models, and reception surrounding Hinton and Minkowski

parts:
You're right to insist on a closer reading. I had substantially underestimated Hinton. **He did not merely speculate about a fourth spatial dimension. He built a recognizably mechanical, physically interpreted four-dimensional model, and he connected it to filamentary matter, the appearance of motion and time, and vortex-based electrodynamics.** The resemblance is considerably more specific than my earlier comparison allowed.

The most striking passage is in *The Fourth Dimension*, first published in 1904, not 1906. Hinton imagines a permanent four-dimensional structure made of filaments. A three-dimensional “film” intersects those structures, and the successive intersections appear to observers as atoms, bodies, and motion. He writes that each atom at each moment is “a new part of that endless line which is itself.” He then says that the apparent motions of the three-dimensional world could arise from “one steady movement of the film as a whole.” <FileCite ref="turn58file10"/>

That is not a casual analogy. It is a geometrical account of how a temporally changing, three-dimensional world could be the sectional appearance of a more extensive spatial structure. Hinton is quite deliberately treating the higher-dimensional world literally. In another passage, he says explicitly that he takes Plato's higher world “literally, not metaphorically.” <FileCite ref="turn58file10"/>

And then the electrical material arrives.

And the chronology makes this much more interesting.

Hinton's first edition was published in **1904**, four years before Minkowski's famous 1908 address. The uploaded 1906 edition preserves that publication history. Hinton's 1903 footnote also refers to his own paper in the *Proceedings of the Royal Irish Academy*, where he had already been working on the geometry of four-dimensional rotations. So this was a developing research programme, not a retrospective interpretation of Minkowski. <FileCite ref="turn58file10"/>

## 1. The 1886 Hinton is already thinking in filaments

The earlier *Scientific Romances* contains a passage I think deserves particular attention.

Hinton constructs a model in which a system of threads is fixed into a complex, interconnected framework. The framework moves through a fluid plane. The intersections of the threads with the plane appear to its inhabitants as moving points, which he calls atoms.

He then imposes four conditions on these apparent particles: permanence, impenetrability, inertia, and conservation of energy. The conditions are not merely philosophical decorations. He uses them to constrain the geometry of the threads.

One detail is especially interesting: **to satisfy his condition of inertia, the threads must be straight between their points of contact.** A curved thread would produce a projected particle whose velocity changed spontaneously. At intersections or contacts, however, the apparent particles can interact and change their motion.

He even derives a mathematical condition involving the sum of the squared tangents of the angles the threads make with the plane's normal. <FileCite ref="turn58file9"/>

There is a very recognizable architecture here:

- Persistent higher-dimensional structures.
- A lower-dimensional intersection producing apparent particles.
- Apparent motion arising from the geometry and orientation of the structures.
- Constraints on the geometry derived from observed physical behavior.
- Interactions occurring where the structures meet.

And notice the relationship to your light/matter distinction. Hinton's straight threads are required to produce inertial motion in the lower-dimensional appearance. Your proposal that light follows straight paths while matter follows more complicated trajectories is not something I can attribute to Hinton, but the underlying concern with the geometry of the path and its observed consequences is already present.

Hinton's 1886 model also says something quite remarkable about causality: from the perspective of the inhabitants of the plane, there would be no cause and effect in the ordinary sense, but the successive realization of an already-existing higher-dimensional structure. <FileCite ref="turn58file9"/>

## 2. The 1906 book makes the connection much stronger

Hinton's later formulation is more developed. He now explicitly calls the complex structures **filaments**.

He considers a spiral intersected by a moving film. The intersection appears as a moving point. He then generalizes from a spiral to complicated structures of filaments, whose intersections with the film constitute the atoms of the observable world.

But here is a subtlety worth preserving: Hinton initially considers the filaments stationary, with the film moving uniformly through them. He then relaxes that assumption and considers the possibility that the filaments themselves move or act.

That gives him two sources of apparent motion:

1. The movement of the film through the underlying structure.
2. Changes in the underlying structure itself.

This is an important distinction. Hinton is not simply saying that all motion is illusion. He is separating the motion associated with the changing section from motion belonging to the more complete structure. <FileCite ref="turn58file10"/>

Your timesheet concept seems to occupy this same conceptual territory, but with an important physical difference: you are proposing a genuinely moving, expanding time surface, with outward propagation from all points. Hinton's principal model is a uniformly advancing three-dimensional section through four-dimensional spatial structure. He does not give us your particular expansion mechanism.

Still, the resemblance is extraordinary.

## 3. Kelvin is not an incidental reference

The vortex chapter is where I think the historical comparison becomes especially consequential.

Hinton begins with Kelvin's hypothesis that matter might consist of portions of fluid segregated into persistent vortices. He recognizes the difficulty of arranging vortex rings and endless vortex filaments in an ether, and proposes that four-dimensional rotation offers a way to imagine a homogeneous vortex-filled medium.

He then develops the mechanics:

- In three dimensions, rotation is around an axis.
- In four dimensions, rotation is around a plane.
- A four-dimensional vortex can therefore be represented as a region of vorticity with a contour, a vortex sheet.
- Several such sheets can form a more extensive structure.

He next connects this geometry to electricity.

Hinton proposes two kinds of double rotation, which he calls A and B. The distinction is geometrically significant: reversing both rotational components preserves the same kind of motion, while reversing only one produces a different kind. He proposes these as possible physical counterparts of positive and negative electricity.

He then combines them into a model of electrical current as a four-dimensional vortex sheet, with the conducting circuit forming its boundary. The action is located in the surrounding medium and the field region, rather than simply being a substance flowing through the wire. <FileCite ref="turn58file10"/>

This is a substantial attempt to explain physical phenomena through the geometry and dynamics of a medium. He is not merely using vortices as an illustration.

There is also a very human and revealing moment in his conclusion. After developing all of this, Hinton admits that a definite conclusion requires investigation of the resultant pressures produced by the collocation of solid vortices and surface vortices.

He stops there.

That is not a trivial omission. It is the point at which the geometry must begin producing quantitative physical consequences. He has proposed a possible geometric identity for electricity and a mechanism for currents, but he has not completed the interaction calculation.

And that is remarkably close to the problem you describe having encountered independently: how do these structures produce the forces between charges?

One qualification: Hinton's model is a *mediated* mechanism through a fluid-like ether, not an unmediated Newtonian action at a distance. He does not derive Coulomb repulsion in the text. The pressure calculation he leaves open might be relevant to such a derivation, but we cannot assume that it would yield the Coulomb law.

There is a particularly interesting quantitative wrinkle. Hinton recognizes that an interaction spreading through four commensurable dimensions would have a different distance dependence from the inverse-square behavior he associates with observed magnetic action. He tries to address this by suggesting that the ether's extent in the fourth direction must be small compared with measurable distances. Whether that proposal actually works is a separate question, but it shows that he understood the need to reconcile the geometry with measured force laws. <FileCite ref="turn58file10"/>

## 4. The forward matter is almost as interesting as the theory

The prefatory material in *A New Era of Thought* is unusually revealing.

Hinton had left England for a foreign appointment, leaving manuscripts with Alicia Boole and H. John Falk. They explain that they were asked to expand the work, but that they had come to believe his philosophical thought lost force when touched by other hands.

They printed Part I almost exactly as he had written it. Part II was reconstructed from a hurried sketch that Hinton himself considered inadequate. They corrected and supplemented it. One chapter was entirely rewritten without his supervision; several appendices and all the exercises were written by the editors.

This matters. The book is not a uniform statement by one author. The provenance of individual arguments is different, and any historical comparison that treats every sentence as Hinton's own would be careless. <FileCite ref="turn58file0"/>

But the editors also give us a glimpse of the actual working culture around him. They insist that four-dimensional geometry cannot be learned from verbal descriptions alone. Readers must construct cubes, arrange models, manipulate sections, and maintain continuous contact with the geometrical facts. They call printing a poor substitute for direct construction.

That is not just an educational preference. It is a methodological conviction.

Hinton himself, in the introductory note, prefers the term **higher matter** to higher space. He says that splitting concrete matter into abstractions such as extension and impenetrability is premature. He wants an intuitive, experimental familiarity with higher-dimensional matter.

Then, in the 1906 preface, he goes even further: mathematical space and the space of real things, which he calls permeable matter, are not necessarily the same subject. A theory is not equivalent to the thing theorized about. <FileCite ref="turn58file0"/> <FileCite ref="turn58file10"/>

That is a surprisingly close philosophical neighbor to your insistence that mathematical consistency does not establish physical possibility.

There is another parallel worth noting. In the 1888 introduction, Hinton says there are no new truths in his book. He is taking leading ideas from Kant, Gauss, and Lobachevsky and trying to make them experientially accessible. He distinguishes the discovery of knowledge from the education of the mind to understand what has already been discovered. <FileCite ref="turn58file0"/>

That sounds rather familiar in the context of your description of SAT as a systematic geometric reconstruction rather than an attempt to invent entirely new physics.

## 5. The reception history provides a clue

The most revealing later source is W. Whately Smith's 1920 book.

Smith knew Hinton's work. He explicitly discusses Hinton's theories of four-dimensional electricity and vortex motion. He calls them highly ingenious, but says he sees no considerable reason to suppose they are more than ingenious speculation. He therefore declines to describe them in detail.

He does, however, outline Hinton's two kinds of four-dimensional rotation and the possible relationship to positive and negative electricity. He even acknowledges that the two kinds might correspond to the two polarities. <FileCite ref="turn58file2"/>

That is a significant historical clue. Hinton's ideas were not simply unknown. They were available to later writers, and at least some of those writers recognized the unusual structure of his argument.

But Smith's book is principally concerned with survival and psychical research. Its preface explicitly describes its proposals as speculative, tentative, and potentially incompatible. Hinton's physical work appears inside a literary and intellectual environment increasingly associated with psychical research and metaphysical speculation.

I would not claim that this alone explains why Hinton's physics did not develop further. It does, however, show how his work could be encountered, acknowledged as ingenious, and then left outside the main line of physical investigation.

Harrow's 1920 popular account of Minkowski provides the other side of the story. He explains that a particle's history is a worldline and that observations are intersections or coincidences of worldlines. He even emphasizes that the complete history is only known through a sequence of such intersections. <FileCite ref="turn58file6"/>

So we have two ideas circulating in the same broad intellectual period:

- Hinton's physical filaments intersected by a moving spatial section.
- Minkowski's worldlines and the events at which they intersect.

They are not identical constructions, but the conceptual overlap is real.

---

## 6. What I now think is the right historical comparison

The collection suggests a much richer picture than my earlier answer did.

| Hinton | SAT, as you have described it |
|---|---|
| Four-dimensional physical space | Four spacelike dimensions |
| Higher-dimensional matter | Physical worldline/filament structures |
| Moving three-dimensional film | Moving time surface or timesheet |
| Intersections appear as atoms and motion | Intersections produce observed particles and events |
| Filaments can interlink and form complex structures | Matter follows nonstraight, coiled, braided trajectories |
| Four-dimensional vortices | Kelvin-vortex geometry as a physical mechanism |
| Two kinds of double rotation as possible charge polarities | Geometric account of charge and interactions |
| Unfinished vortex pressure calculation | Your unresolved Coulomb interaction problem |

The strongest similarities are structural, not terminological. Hinton has already assembled several of the same pieces into one physical picture.

But I see three especially important differences.

**First, the geometry of time.** Hinton's model is primarily a spatial four-dimensional structure through which a three-dimensional section advances. SAT makes the propagation of the fourth spatial direction itself the physical process perceived as time, with expansion outward from all points. That is a more specific dynamical hypothesis.

**Second, the distinction between matter and light.** Hinton's straight threads are part of his explanation of inertia, but he does not develop your proposal that light leaves matter behind along a straight path while matter itself follows more complicated trajectories. That is a potentially distinct piece of SAT.

**Third, the force problem.** Hinton gets as far as geometric polarity, vortex-mediated electrical phenomena, and unresolved pressure interactions. He does not get to a completed quantitative theory of Coulomb repulsion, much less a complete derivation of electromagnetic and gravitational interactions from a common filament geometry.

And there is one important historical distinction: Minkowski's formalism does not simply make time an ordinary fourth spatial coordinate. Its Lorentzian metric distinguishes temporal and spatial directions. The historical use of an imaginary time coordinate, \(ict\), was a way of expressing that geometry, not merely a cosmetic alteration. SAT's four-spacelike-dimensional proposal therefore has to account for the observed Lorentzian causal structure, not simply discard it. But Hinton's work demonstrates that a physically literal fourth spatial dimension was already being explored before Minkowski's synthesis.

## 7. The subtext I find most significant

Hinton seems to have been trying to do something that was difficult to place in the intellectual categories of his time.

He wanted four-dimensional space to be physically real, but he didn't want to approach it exclusively through mathematics. He wanted it to be mechanically intelligible, but his preferred method was construction, observation, and intuition. He wanted to explain microscopic physics, but he also saw higher-dimensional geometry as a route into consciousness, life, social organization, and the relationship between parts and wholes.

He was not simply a mathematician writing about an abstract dimension. He was trying to change what people could *see* and *think* through direct manipulation of geometrical models.

The human details reinforce this: collaborators physically making models, a publisher who understood his work well enough to support it, editors who protected his voice while acknowledging the limits of their reconstruction, and later writers who recognized the ingenuity but did not pursue the physical implications.

I would put it this way:

**Hinton had much of the architecture. He did not complete the physics.**

And the most interesting possibility is that you independently arrived at a closely related architecture by pursuing a different route, then encountered the same unresolved problem that Hinton had left sitting at the edge of his own construction.

[L19] ALBERT EINSTEIN



[L23] NOBEL LECTURE



[L27] FUNDAMENTAL IDEAS AND PROBLEMS
[L28] OF THE THEORY OF RELATIVITY



[L32] Lecture delivered to the Nordic Assembly of Naturalists at Gothenburg,[1] July 11, 1923.





[L38] If we consider that part of the theory of relativity which may nowadays in a sense be regarded as bona fide scientific knowledge, we note two aspects which have a major bearing on this theory. The whole development of the theory turns on the question of whether there are physically preferred states of motion in Nature (physical relativity problem). Also, concepts and distinctions are only admissible to the extent that observable facts can be assigned to them without ambiguity (stipulation that concepts and distinctions should have meaning). This postulate, pertaining to epistemology, proves to be of fundamental importance.

[L40] These two aspects become clear when applied to a special case, e.g. to classical mechanics. Firstly we see that at any point filled with matter there exists a preferred state of motion, namely that of the substance at the point considered. Our problem starts however with the question whether physically preferred states of motion exist in reference to extensiveregions. From the viewpoint of classical mechanics the answer is in the affirmative; the physically preferred states of motion from the viewpoint of mechanics are those of the inertial frames.

[L42] This assertion, in common with the basis of the whole of mechanics as it generally used to be described before the relativity theory, far from meets the above "stipulation of meaning". Motion can only be conceived as the relative motion of bodies. In mechanics, motion relative to the system of coordinates is implied when merely motion is referred to. Nevertheless this interpretation does not comply with the "stipulation of meaning" if the coordinate system is considered as something purely imaginary. If we turn our attention to experimental physics we see that there the coordinate system is invariably represented by a "practically rigid" body. Furthermore it is assumed that such rigid bodies can be positioned in rest relative to one another in common with the bodies of Euclidian geometry. Insofar as we may think of the rigid measuring body as existing as an object which can be experienced, the "system of coordinates" concept as well as the concept of the motion of matter relative thereto can be accepted in the sense of the "stipulation of meaning". At the same time Euclidian geometry, by this conception, has been adapted to the requirements of the physics of the "stipulation of meaning". The question whether Euclidian geometry is valid becomes physically significant; its validity is assumed in classical physics and also later in the special theory of relativity.

[L44] In classical mechanics the inertial frame and time are best defined together by a suitable formulation of the law of inertia: It is possible to fix the time and assign a state of motion to the system of coordinates (inertial frame) such that, with reference to the latter, force-free material points undergo no acceleration; furthermore it is assumed that this time can be measured without disagreement by identical clocks (systems which run down periodically) in any arbitrary state of motion. There are then an infinite number of inertial frames which are in uniform translational motion relative to each other, and hence there is also an infinite number of mutually equivalent, physically preferred states of motion. Time is absolute, i.e. independent of the choice of the particular inertial frame; it is defined by more characteristics than logically necessary, although—as implied by mechanics—this should not lead to contradictions with experience. Note in passing that the logical weakness of this exposition from the point of view of the stipulation of meaning is the lack of an experimental criterion for whether a material point is force-free or not; therefore the concept of the inertial frame remains rather problematical. This deficiency leads to the general theory of relativity. We shall not consider it for the moment.

[L46] The concept of the rigid body (and that of the clock) has a key bearing on the foregoing consideration of the fundamentals of mechanics, a bearing which there is some justification for challenging. The rigid body is only approximately achieved in Nature, not even with desired approximation; this concept does not therefore strictly satisfy the "stipulation of meaning". It is also logically unjustifiable to base all physical consideration on the rigid or solid body and then finally reconstruct that body atomically by means of elementary physical laws which in turn have been determined by means of the rigid measuring body. I am mentioning these deficiencies of method because in the same sense they are also a feature of the relativity theory in the schematic exposition which I am advocating here. Certainly it would be logically more correct to begin with the whole of the laws and to apply the "stipulation of meaning" to this whole first, i.e. to put the unambiguous relation to the world of experience last instead of already fulfilling it in an imperfect form for an artificially isolated part, namely the space-time metric. We are not, however, sufficiently advanced in our knowledge of Nature's elementary laws to adopt this more perfect method without going out of our depth. At the close of our considerations we shall see that in the most recent studies there is an attempt, based on ideas by Levi-Civita, Weyl, and Eddington, to implement that logically purer method.

[L48] It more clearly follows from the above what is implied by "preferred states of motion". They are preferred as regards the laws of Nature. States of motion are preferred when, relative to the formulation of the laws of Nature, coordinate systems within them are distinguished in that with respect to them those laws assume a form preferred by simplicity. According to classical mechanics the states of motion of the inertial frames in this sense are physically preferred. Classical mechanics permits a distinction to be made between (absolutely) unaccelerated and accelerated motions; it also claims that velocities have only a relative existence (dependent on the selection of the inertial frame), while accelerations and rotations have an absolute existence (independent of the selection of the inertial frame). This state of affairs can be expressed thus: According to classical mechanics "velocity relativity" exists, but not "acceleration relativity". After these preliminary considerations we can pass to the actual topic of our contemplations, the relativity theory, by characterizing its development so far in terms of principles.

[L50] The special theory of relativity is an adaptation of physical principles to Maxwell-Lorentz electrodynamics. From earlier physics it takes the assumption that Euclidian geometry is valid for the laws governing the position of rigid bodies, the inertial frame and the law of inertia. The postulate of equivalence of inertial frames for the formulation of the laws of Nature is assumed to be valid for the whole of physics (special relativity principle). From Maxwell-Lorentz electrodynamics it takes the postulate of invariance of the velocity of light in a vacuum (light principle).

[L52] To harmonize the relativity principle with the light principle, the assumption that an absolute time (agreeing for all inertial frames) exists, had to be abandoned. Thus the hypothesis is abandoned that arbitrarily moved and suitably set identical clocks function in such a way that the times shown by two of them, which meet, agree. A specific time is assigned to each inertial frame; the state of motion and the time of the inertial frame are defined, in accordance with the stipulation of meaning, by the requirement that the light principle should apply to it. The existence of the inertial frame thus defined and the validity of the law of inertia with respect to it are assumed. The time for each inertial frame is measured by identical clocks that are stationary relative to the frame.

[L54] The laws of transformation for space coordinates and time for the transition from one inertial frame to another, the Lorentz transformations as they are termed, are unequivocally established by these definitions and the hypotheses concealed in the assumption that they are free from contradiction. Their immediate physical significance lies in the effect of the motion relative to the used inertial frame on the form of rigid bodies (Lorentz contraction) and on the rate of the clocks. According to the special relativity principle the laws of Nature must be covariant relative to Lorentz transformations; the theory thus provides a criterion for general laws of Nature. It leads in particular to a modification of the Newtonian point motion law in which the velocity of light in a vacuum is considered the limiting velocity, and it also leads to the realization that energy and inertial mass are of like nature.

[L56] The special relativity theory resulted in appreciable advances. It reconciled mechanics and electrodynamics. It reduced the number of logically independent hypotheses regarding the latter. It enforced the need for a clarification of the fundamental concepts in epistemological terms. It united the momentum and energy principle, and demonstrated the like nature of mass and energy. Yet it was not entirely satisfactory—quite apart from the quantum problems, which all theory so far has been incapable of really solving. In common with classical mechanics the special relativity theory favours certain states of motion—namely those of the inertial frames—to all other states of motion. This was actually more difficult to tolerate than the preference for a single state of motion as in the case of the theory of light with a stationary ether, for this imagined a real reason for the preference, i.e. the light ether. A theory which from the outset prefers no state of motion should appear more satisfactory. Moreover the previously mentioned vagueness in the definition of the inertial frame or in the formulation of the law of inertia raises doubts which obtain their decisive importance, owing to the empirical principle for the equality of the inertial and heavy mass, in the light of the following consideration.

[L58] Let  be an inertial frame without a gravitational field, ' a system of coordinates accelerated uniformly relative to . The behaviour of material points relative to ' is the same as if ' were an inertial frame in respect of which a homogeneous gravitational field exists. On the basis of the empirically known properties of the gravitational field, the definition of the inertial frame thus proves to be weak. The conclusion is obvious that any arbitrarily moved frame of reference is equivalent to any other for the formulation of the laws of Nature, that there are thus no physically preferred states of motion at all in respect of regions of finite extension (general relativity principle).

[L60] The implementation of this concept necessitates an even more profound modification of the geometric-kinematical principles than the special relativity theory. The Lorentz contraction, which is derived from the latter, leads to the conclusion that with regard to a system ' arbitrarily moved relative to a (gravity field free) inertial frame , the laws of Euclidian geometry governing the position of rigid (at rest relative to ' bodies do not apply. Consequently the Cartesian system of coordinates also loses its significance in terms of the stipulation of meaning. Analogous reasoning applies to time; with reference to ' the time can no longer meaningfully be defined by the indication on identical clocks at rest relative to ', nor by the law governing the propagation of light. Generalizing, we arrive at the conclusion that gravitational field and metric are only different manifestations of the same physical field.

[L62] We arrive at the formal description of this field by the following consideration. For each infinitesimal point-environment in an arbitrary gravitational field a local frame of coordinates can be given for such a state of motion that relative to this local frame no gravitational field exists (local inertial frame). In terms of this inertial frame we may regard the results of the special relativity theory as correct to a first approximation for this infinitesimally small region. There are an infinite number of such local inertial frames at any space-time point; they are associated by Lorentz transformations. [L64] ETHER AND THE THEORY OF RELATIVITY

[L66] An Address delivered on May 5th, 1920, in the University of Leyden



[L70] How does it come about that alongside of the idea of ponderable
[L71] matter, which is derived by abstraction from everyday life, the
[L72] physicists set the idea of the existence of another kind of matter,
[L73] the ether? The explanation is probably to be sought in those phenomena
[L74] which have given rise to the theory of action at a distance, and
[L75] in the properties of light which have led to the undulatory theory.
[L76] Let us devote a little while to the consideration of these two
[L77] subjects.

[L79] Outside of physics we know nothing of action at a distance. When
[L80] we try to connect cause and effect in the experiences which natural
[L81] objects afford us, it seems at first as if there were no other mutual
[L82] actions than those of immediate contact, e.g. the communication of
[L83] motion by impact, push and pull, heating or inducing combustion by
[L84] means of a flame, etc. It is true that even in everyday experience
[L85] weight, which is in a sense action at a distance, plays a very
[L86] important part. But since in daily experience the weight of bodies
[L87] meets us as something constant, something not linked to any cause
[L88] which is variable in time or place, we do not in everyday life
[L89] speculate as to the cause of gravity, and therefore do not become
[L90] conscious of its character as action at a distance. It was Newton's
[L91] theory of gravitation that first assigned a cause for gravity by
[L92] interpreting it as action at a distance, proceeding from masses.
[L93] Newton's theory is probably the greatest stride ever made in
[L94] the effort towards the causal nexus of natural phenomena. And yet
[L95] this theory evoked a lively sense of discomfort among Newton's
[L96] contemporaries, because it seemed to be in conflict with the
[L97] principle springing from the rest of experience, that there can be
[L98] reciprocal action only through contact, and not through immediate
[L99] action at a distance. It is only with reluctance that man's desire
[L100] for knowledge endures a dualism of this kind. How was unity to
[L101] be preserved in his comprehension of the forces of nature? Either
[L102] by trying to look upon contact forces as being themselves distant
[L103] forces which admittedly are observable only at a very small
[L104] distance--and this was the road which Newton's followers, who were
[L105] entirely under the spell of his doctrine, mostly preferred to
[L106] take; or by assuming that the Newtonian action at a distance is
[L107] only _apparently_ immediate action at a distance, but in truth is
[L108] conveyed by a medium permeating space, whether by movements or by
[L109] elastic deformation of this medium. Thus the endeavour toward a
[L110] unified view of the nature of forces leads to the hypothesis of an
[L111] ether. This hypothesis, to be sure, did not at first bring with it
[L112] any advance in the theory of gravitation or in physics generally,
[L113] so that it became customary to treat Newton's law of force as an
[L114] axiom not further reducible. But the ether hypothesis was bound
[L115] always to play some part in physical science, even if at first only
[L116] a latent part.

[L118] When in the first half of the nineteenth century the far-reaching
[L119] similarity was revealed which subsists between the properties of
[L120] light and those of elastic waves in ponderable bodies, the ether
[L121] hypothesis found fresh support. It appeared beyond question that
[L122] light must be interpreted as a vibratory process in an elastic, inert
[L123] medium filling up universal space. It also seemed to be a necessary
[L124] consequence of the fact that light is capable of polarisation that
[L125] this medium, the ether, must be of the nature of a solid body,
[L126] because transverse waves are not possible in a fluid, but only in
[L127] a solid. Thus the physicists were bound to arrive at the theory
[L128] of the "quasi-rigid" luminiferous ether, the parts of which can
[L129] carry out no movements relatively to one another except the small
[L130] movements of deformation which correspond to light-waves.

[L132] This theory--also called the theory of the stationary luminiferous
[L133] ether--moreover found a strong support in an experiment which is
[L134] also of fundamental importance in the special theory of relativity,
[L135] the experiment of Fizeau, from which one was obliged to infer
[L136] that the luminiferous ether does not take part in the movements of
[L137] bodies. The phenomenon of aberration also favoured the theory of
[L138] the quasi-rigid ether.

[L140] The development of the theory of electricity along the path opened
[L141] up by Maxwell and Lorentz gave the development of our ideas concerning
[L142] the ether quite a peculiar and unexpected turn. For Maxwell himself
[L143] the ether indeed still had properties which were purely mechanical,
[L144] although of a much more complicated kind than the mechanical
[L145] properties of tangible solid bodies. But neither Maxwell nor his
[L146] followers succeeded in elaborating a mechanical model for the ether
[L147] which might furnish a satisfactory mechanical interpretation of
[L148] Maxwell's laws of the electro-magnetic field. The laws were clear
[L149] and simple, the mechanical interpretations clumsy and contradictory.
[L150] Almost imperceptibly the theoretical physicists adapted themselves
[L151] to a situation which, from the standpoint of their mechanical
[L152] programme, was very depressing. They were particularly influenced
[L153] by the electro-dynamical investigations of Heinrich Hertz. For
[L154] whereas they previously had required of a conclusive theory that
[L155] it should content itself with the fundamental concepts which belong
[L156] exclusively to mechanics (e.g. densities, velocities, deformations,
[L157] stresses) they gradually accustomed themselves to admitting electric and
[L158] magnetic force as fundamental concepts side by side with those of
[L159] mechanics, without requiring a mechanical interpretation for them.
[L160] Thus the purely mechanical view of nature was gradually abandoned.
[L161] But this change led to a fundamental dualism which in the long-run
[L162] was insupportable. A way of escape was now sought in the reverse
[L163] direction, by reducing the principles of mechanics to those
[L164] of electricity, and this especially as confidence in the strict
[L165] validity of the equations of Newton's mechanics was shaken by the
[L166] experiments with beta-rays and rapid kathode rays.

[L168] This dualism still confronts us in unextenuated form in the theory
[L169] of Hertz, where matter appears not only as the bearer of velocities,
[L170] kinetic energy, and mechanical pressures, but also as the bearer of
[L171] electromagnetic fields. Since such fields also occur _in vacuo_--i.e.
[L172] in free ether--the ether also appears as bearer of electromagnetic
[L173] fields. The ether appears indistinguishable in its functions from
[L174] ordinary matter. Within matter it takes part in the motion of matter
[L175] and in empty space it has everywhere a velocity; so that the ether
[L176] has a definitely assigned velocity throughout the whole of space.
[L177] There is no fundamental difference between Hertz's ether and
[L178] ponderable matter (which in part subsists in the ether).

[L180] The Hertz theory suffered not only from the defect of ascribing
[L181] to matter and ether, on the one hand mechanical states, and on the
[L182] other hand electrical states, which do not stand in any conceivable
[L183] relation to each other; it was also at variance with the result of
[L184] Fizeau's important experiment on the velocity of the propagation
[L185] of light in moving fluids, and with other established experimental
[L186] results.

[L188] Such was the state of things when H. A. Lorentz entered upon the
[L189] scene. He brought theory into harmony with experience by means of
[L190] a wonderful simplification of theoretical principles. He achieved
[L191] this, the most important advance in the theory of electricity since
[L192] Maxwell, by taking from ether its mechanical, and from matter its
[L193] electromagnetic qualities. As in empty space, so too in the interior
[L194] of material bodies, the ether, and not matter viewed atomistically,
[L195] was exclusively the seat of electromagnetic fields. According to
[L196] Lorentz the elementary particles of matter alone are capable of
[L197] carrying out movements; their electromagnetic activity is entirely
[L198] confined to the carrying of electric charges. Thus Lorentz succeeded
[L199] in reducing all electromagnetic happenings to Maxwell's equations
[L200] for free space.

[L202] As to the mechanical nature of the Lorentzian ether, it may be said
[L203] of it, in a somewhat playful spirit, that immobility is the only
[L204] mechanical property of which it has not been deprived by H. A.
[L205] Lorentz. It may be added that the whole change in the conception
[L206] of the ether which the special theory of relativity brought about,
[L207] consisted in taking away from the ether its last mechanical quality,
[L208] namely, its immobility. How this is to be understood will forthwith
[L209] be expounded.

[L211] The space-time theory and the kinematics of the special theory
[L212] of relativity were modelled on the Maxwell-Lorentz theory of the
[L213] electromagnetic field. This theory therefore satisfies the conditions
[L214] of the special theory of relativity, but when viewed from the latter
[L215] it acquires a novel aspect. For if K be a system of co-ordinates
[L216] relatively to which the Lorentzian ether is at rest, the
[L217] Maxwell-Lorentz equations are valid primarily with reference to K.
[L218] But by the special theory of relativity the same equations without
[L219] any change of meaning also hold in relation to any new system of
[L220] co-ordinates K' which is moving in uniform translation relatively
[L221] to K. Now comes the anxious question:--Why must I in the theory
[L222] distinguish the K system above all K' systems, which are physically
[L223] equivalent to it in all respects, by assuming that the ether
[L224] is at rest relatively to the K system? For the theoretician such
[L225] an asymmetry in the theoretical structure, with no corresponding
[L226] asymmetry in the system of experience, is intolerable. If we assume
[L227] the ether to be at rest relatively to K, but in motion relatively
[L228] to K', the physical equivalence of K and K' seems to me from the
[L229] logical standpoint, not indeed downright incorrect, but nevertheless
[L230] inacceptable.

[L232] The next position which it was possible to take up in face of this
[L233] state of things appeared to be the following. The ether does not
[L234] exist at all. The electromagnetic fields are not states of a medium,
[L235] and are not bound down to any bearer, but they are independent
[L236] realities which are not reducible to anything else, exactly like
[L237] the atoms of ponderable matter. This conception suggests itself
[L238] the more readily as, according to Lorentz's theory, electromagnetic
[L239] radiation, like ponderable matter, brings impulse and energy with
[L240] it, and as, according to the special theory of relativity, both
[L241] matter and radiation are but special forms of distributed energy,
[L242] ponderable mass losing its isolation and appearing as a special
[L243] form of energy.

[L245] More careful reflection teaches us, however, that the special theory
[L246] of relativity does not compel us to deny ether. We may assume the
[L247] existence of an ether; only we must give up ascribing a definite
[L248] state of motion to it, i.e. we must by abstraction take from it the
[L249] last mechanical characteristic which Lorentz had still left it. We
[L250] shall see later that this point of view, the conceivability of which
[L251] I shall at once endeavour to make more intelligible by a somewhat
[L252] halting comparison, is justified by the results of the general
[L253] theory of relativity.

[L130]                         HISTORICAL INTRODUCTION


[L133] Lord Kelvin writing in 1893, in his preface to the English edition of
[L134] Hertz’s Researches on Electric Waves, says “many workers and many
[L135] thinkers have helped to build up the nineteenth century school of
[L136] _plenum_, one ether for light, heat, electricity, magnetism; and the
[L137] German and English volumes containing Hertz’s electrical papers, given
[L138] to the world in the last decade of the century, will be a permanent
[L139] monument of the splendid consummation now realised.”

[L141] Ten years later, in 1905, we find Einstein declaring that “the ether
[L142] will be proved to be superfluous.” At first sight the revolution in
[L143] scientific thought brought about in the course of a single decade
[L144] appears to be almost too violent. A more careful even though a rapid
[L145] review of the subject will, however, show how the Theory of Relativity
[L146] gradually became a historical necessity.

[L148] Towards the beginning of the nineteenth century, the luminiferous ether
[L149] came into prominence as a result of the brilliant successes of the wave
[L150] theory in the hands of Young and Fresnel. In its stationary aspect the
[L151] elastic solid ether was the outcome of the search for a medium in which
[L152] the light waves may “undulate.” This stationary ether, as shown by
[L153] Young, also afforded a satisfactory explanation of astronomical
[L154] aberration. But its very success gave rise to a host of new questions
[L155] all bearing on the central problem of relative motion of ether and
[L156] matter.

[L158] _Arago’s prism experiment._—The refractive index of a glass prism
[L159] depends on the incident velocity of light outside the prism and its
[L160] velocity inside the prism after refraction. On Fresnel’s fixed ether
[L161] hypothesis, the incident light waves are situated in the stationary
[L162] ether outside the prism and move with velocity _c_ with respect to the
[L163] ether. If the prism moves with a velocity _u_ with respect to this fixed
[L164] ether, then the incident velocity of light with respect to the prism
[L165] should be _c_ + _u_. Thus the refractive index of the glass prism should
[L166] depend on _u_ the absolute velocity of the prism, _i.e._, its velocity
[L167] with respect to the fixed ether. Arago performed the experiment in 1819,
[L168] but failed to detect the expected change.

[L170] _Airy-Boscovitch water-telescope experiment._—Boscovitch had still
[L171] earlier in 1766, raised the very important question of the dependence of
[L172] aberration on the refractive index of the medium filling the telescope.
[L173] Aberration depends on the difference in the velocity of light outside
[L174] the telescope and its velocity inside the telescope. If the latter
[L175] velocity changes owing to a change in the medium filling the telescope,
[L176] aberration itself should change, that is, aberration should depend on
[L177] the nature of the medium.

[L179] Airy, in 1871 filled up a telescope with water—but failed to detect any
[L180] change in the aberration. Thus we get both in the case of Arago prism
[L181] experiment and Airy-Boscovitch water-telescope experiment, the very
[L182] startling result that optical effects in a moving medium seem to be
[L183] quite independent of the velocity of the medium with respect to
[L184] Fresnel’s stationary ether.

[L186] _Fresnel’s convection coefficient k = 1 - 1/μ^2._—Possibly some form
[L187] of compensation is taking place. Working on this hypothesis, Fresnel
[L188] offered his famous ether convection theory. According to Fresnel, the
[L189] presence of matter implies a definite condensation of ether within the
[L190] region occupied by matter. This “condensed” or excess portion of ether
[L191] is supposed to be carried away with its own piece of moving matter. It
[L192] should be observed that only the “excess” portion is carried away,
[L193] while the rest remains as stagnant as ever. A complete convection of
[L194] the “excess” ether ρ′ with the full velocity _u_ is optically
[L195] equivalent to a partial convection of the total ether ρ, with only a
[L196] fraction of the velocity _k_. _u_. Fresnel showed that if this
[L197] convection coefficient _k_ is 1 - 1/μ^2 (μ being the refractive index
[L198] of the prism), then the velocity of light after refraction within the
[L199] moving prism would be altered to just such extent as would make the
[L200] refractive index of the moving prism quite independent of its
[L201] “absolute” velocity _u_. The non-dependence of aberration on the
[L202] “absolute” velocity _u_, is also very easily explained with the help
[L203] of this Fresnelian convection-coefficient _k_.

[L205] _Stokes’ viscous ether._—It should be remembered, however, that
[L206] Fresnel’s stationary ether is absolutely fixed and is not at all
[L207] disturbed by the motion of matter through it. In this respect Fresnelian
[L208] ether cannot be said to behave in any respectable physical fashion, and
[L209] this led Stokes, in 1845-46, to construct a more material type of
[L210] medium. Stokes assumed that viscous motion ensues near the surface of
[L211] separation of ether and moving matter, while at sufficiently distant
[L212] regions the ether remains wholly undisturbed. He showed how such a
[L213] viscous ether would explain aberration if all motion in it were
[L214] differentially irrotational. But in order to explain the null Arago
[L215] effect, Stokes was compelled to assume the convection hypothesis of
[L216] Fresnel with an identical numerical value for _k_, namely 1 - 1/μ^2.
[L217] Thus the prestige of the Fresnelian convection-coefficient was enhanced,
[L218] if anything, by the theoretical investigations of Stokes.

[L220] _Fizeau’s experiment._—Soon after, in 1851, it received direct
[L221] experimental confirmation in a brilliant piece of work by Fizeau.

[L223] If a divided beam of light is re-united after passing through two
[L224] adjacent cylinders filled with water, ordinary interference fringes will
[L225] be produced. If the water in one of the cylinders is now made to flow,
[L226] the “condensed” ether within the flowing water would be convected and
[L227] would produce a shift in the interference fringes. The shift actually
[L228] observed agreed very well with a value of k = 1 - 1/μ^2. The Fresnelian
[L229] convection-coefficient now became firmly established as a consequence of
[L230] a direct positive effect. On the other hand, the negative evidences in
[L231] favour of the convection-coefficient had also multiplied. Mascart, Hoek,
[L232] Maxwell and others sought for definite changes in different optical
[L233] effects induced by the motion of the earth relative to the stationary
[L234] ether. But all such attempts failed to reveal the slightest trace of any
[L235] optical disturbance due to the “absolute” velocity of the earth, thus
[L236] proving conclusively that all the different optical effects shared in
[L237] the general compensation arising out of the Fresnelian convection of the
[L238] excess ether. It must be carefully noted that the Fresnelian
[L239] convection-coefficient implicitly assumes the existence of a fixed ether
[L240] (Fresnel) or at least a wholly stagnant medium at sufficiently distant
[L241] regions (Stokes), with reference to which alone a convection velocity
[L242] can have any significance. Thus the convection-coefficient implying some
[L243] type of a stationary or viscous, yet nevertheless “absolute” ether,
[L244] succeeded in explaining satisfactorily all known optical facts down to
1880.

[L247] _Michelson-Morley Experiment._—In 1881, Michelson and Morley performed
[L248] their classical experiments which undermined the whole structure of the
[L249] old ether theory and thus served to introduce the new theory of
[L250] relativity. The fundamental idea underlying this experiment is quite
[L251] simple. In all old experiments the velocity of light situated in free
[L252] ether was compared with the velocity of waves actually situated in a
[L253] piece of moving matter and presumably carried away by it. The
[L254] compensatory effect of the Fresnelian convection of ether afforded a
[L255] satisfactory explanation of all negative results.

[L257] In the Michelson-Morley experiment the arrangement is quite different.
[L258] If there is a definite gap in a rigid body, light waves situated in free
[L259] ether will take a definite time in crossing the gap. If the rigid
[L260] platform carrying the gap is set in motion with respect to the ether in
[L261] the direction of light propagation, light waves (which are even now
[L262] situated in free ether) should presumably take a longer time to cross
[L263] the gap.

[L137] Gewiß hast auch du, lieber Leser, als Knabe oder Mädchen mit dem

[L159] Methoden der Geometrie nicht beantwortbar, sondern überhaupt an sich
[L160] ohne Sinn ist. Man kann nicht fragen, ob es wahr sei, daß durch zwei
[L161] Punkte nur +eine+ Gerade hindurchgeht. Man kann nur sagen, daß die
[L162] Euklidische Geometrie von Gebilden handelt, die sie „Gerade“ nennt, und

[L167] pflegen; die Geometrie aber befaßt sich nicht mit der Beziehung ihrer

[L169] logischen Zusammenhang dieser Begriffe untereinander.

[L171] Daß wir uns trotzdem dazu hingezogen fühlen, die Sätze der Geometrie
[L172] als „wahr“ zu bezeichnen, erklärt sich leicht. Den geometrischen
[L173] Begriffen entsprechen mehr oder weniger exakt Gegenstände in der

[L175] Entstehung jener Begriffe sind. Mag die Geometrie, um ihrem Gebäude
[L176] die größtmögliche logische Geschlossenheit zu geben, hiervon Abstand
[L177] nehmen; die Gewohnheit, beispielsweise in einer Strecke zwei markierte

[L185] Geometrie den einzigen Satz zufügen, daß zwei Punkten eines praktisch
[L186] starren Körpers stets die nämliche Entfernung (Strecke) entspreche, was
