[L1] {
[L2]   "content": "name: Maintain H(s)H navigation

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths-ignore:
      - "indexes/STRUCTURAL_INDEX.md"
      - "indexes/index-state.json"
      - "indexes/CONVERSATION_CHRONOLOGY.md"
      - "indexes/LIVE_CONVERSATION_CHRONOLOGY.md"
      - "indexes/manifests/**"
      - "indexes/autotag/**"
      - "CONVERSATION_VIEWER/data/conversations.json"
      - "CONVERSATION_VIEWER/data/curated/**"

permissions:
  contents: write
  pages: write
  id-token: write

concurrency:
  group: hsh-navigation-main
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  maintain:
    if: ${{ github.event_name != 'push' || !contains(github.event.head_commit.message, '[skip hsh-maintenance]') }}
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 45

    steps:
      - name: Check out current main branch
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          ref: main
          fetch-depth: 0

      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

      - name: Date-tag stable developmental exports
        id: development_dates
        continue-on-error: true
        run: |
          mkdir -p indexes/manifests
          if [ -d "DEVELOPMENT_FULL_CONVOS" ]; then
            python tools/date_conversation_exports.py \
              "DEVELOPMENT_FULL_CONVOS" \
              --apply \
              --resolve-collisions \
              --manifest indexes/manifests/development-conversation-dates.json
          else
            echo "DEVELOPMENT_FULL_CONVOS not present; skipping"
          fi

      - name: Date-tag LIVE CONVOS preserving original source content
        id: live_dates
        continue-on-error: true
        run: |
          mkdir -p indexes/manifests
          if [ -d "LIVE CONVOS" ]; then
            python tools/date_conversation_exports.py \
              "LIVE CONVOS" \
              --apply \
              --resolve-collisions \
              --manifest indexes/manifests/live-conversation-dates.json
          else
            echo "LIVE CONVOS not present; skipping"
          fi

      - name: Verify every datable source now has the right filename date prefix
        run: python tools/audit_conversation_date_tags.py --output indexes/manifests/date-tag-audit.json --strict

      - name: Build conversation viewer from the fresh manifests
        run: python tools/build_conversation_viewer_resolved.py

      - name: Build conversation chronology indexes
        run: |
          if [ -d "DEVELOPMENT_FULL_CONVOS" ]; then
            python tools/index_conversation_chronology.py \
              "DEVELOPMENT_FULL_CONVOS" \
              --output indexes/CONVERSATION_CHRONOLOGY.md
          fi
          if [ -d "LIVE CONVOS" ]; then
            python tools/index_conversation_chronology.py \
              "LIVE CONVOS" \
              --output indexes/LIVE_CONVERSATION_CHRONOLOGY.md
          fi

      - name: Refresh repository structural index before tag cross-check
        run: python tools/index_archive.py --root .

      - name: Build archive-wide conversation autotag indexes
        run: |
          mkdir -p WORKSPACES/COMMON/analysis indexes/autotag
          python WORKSPACES/COMMON/scripts/layered_autotag_nathan_v3.py . \
            --out WORKSPACES/COMMON/analysis/archive_layered_autotags.jsonl \
            --summary indexes/autotag/AUTOTAG_SUMMARY.md \
            --index indexes/autotag/CONVERSATION_TAG_INDEX.md \
            --manifest indexes/autotag/conversation-tag-manifest.json \
            --user-tag-index indexes/autotag/user-message-tags.jsonl \
            --structural-index-state indexes/index-state.json \
            --window 4

      - name: Refresh structural index with autotag surfaces included
        run: python tools/index_archive.py --root .

      - name: Validate Python tooling
        run: |
          python -m py_compile WORKSPACES/COMMON/scripts/layered_autotag_nathan.py
          python -m py_compile WORKSPACES/COMMON/scripts/layered_autotag_nathan_v2.py
          python -m py_compile WORKSPACES/COMMON/scripts/layered_autotag_nathan_v3.py

      - name: Validate viewer JavaScript
        run: |
          node --check CONVERSATION_VIEWER/annotations.js
          node --check CONVERSATION_VIEWER/viewer.js
          node --check CONVERSATION_VIEWER/argus_followup.js
          node --check CONVERSATION_VIEWER/provenance_search.js
          node --check CONVERSATION_VIEWER/landmarks.js
          node --check CONVERSATION_VIEWER/presentation.js

      - name: Run repository tests
        run: python -m unittest discover -s tests -v

      - name: Validate generated navigation state
        run: |
          python -m json.tool indexes/index-state.json >/dev/null
          if [ -f indexes/manifests/development-conversation-dates.json ]; then
            python -m json.tool indexes/manifests/development-conversation-dates.json >/dev/null
          fi
          if [ -f indexes/manifests/live-conversation-dates.json ]; then

          TARGET='SOURCE_INVENTORY/SABLE/source_inventory_run'

            fi

            echo "Push race on attempt ${attempt}; discarding generated commit and retrying from latest main." >&2
            sleep $((attempt * 2))
          done

          exit 1

[L2]   "content": "name: Maintain H(s)H navigation

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths-ignore:
      - "indexes/STRUCTURAL_INDEX.md"
      - "indexes/index-state.json"
      - "indexes/CONVERSATION_CHRONOLOGY.md"
      - "indexes/LIVE_CONVERSATION_CHRONOLOGY.md"
      - "indexes/manifests/**"
      - "indexes/autotag/**"
      - "CONVERSATION_VIEWER/data/conversations.json"
      - "CONVERSATION_VIEWER/data/curated/**"

permissions:
  contents: write
  pages: write
  id-token: write

concurrency:
  group: hsh-navigation-main
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  maintain:
    if: ${{ github.event_name != 'push' || !contains(github.event.head_commit.message, '[skip hsh-maintenance]') }}
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 45

    steps:
      - name: Check out current main branch
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          ref: main
          fetch-depth: 0

      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

      - name: Date-tag stable developmental exports
        id: development_dates
        continue-on-error: true
        run: |
          mkdir -p indexes/manifests
          if [ -d "DEVELOPMENT_FULL_CONVOS" ]; then
            python tools/date_conversation_exports.py \
              "DEVELOPMENT_FULL_CONVOS" \
              --apply \
              --resolve-collisions \
              --manifest indexes/manifests/development-conversation-dates.json
          else
            echo "DEVELOPMENT_FULL_CONVOS not present; skipping"
          fi

      - name: Date-tag LIVE CONVOS preserving original source content
        id: live_dates
        continue-on-error: true
        run: |
          mkdir -p indexes/manifests
          if [ -d "LIVE CONVOS" ]; then
            python tools/date_conversation_exports.py \
              "LIVE CONVOS" \
              --apply \
              --resolve-collisions \
              --manifest indexes/manifests/live-conversation-dates.json
          else
            echo "LIVE CONVOS not present; skipping"
          fi

      - name: Verify every datable source now has the right filename date prefix
        run: python tools/audit_conversation_date_tags.py --output indexes/manifests/date-tag-audit.json --strict

      - name: Build conversation viewer from the fresh manifests
        run: python tools/build_conversation_viewer_resolved.py

      - name: Build conversation chronology indexes
        run: |
          if [ -d "DEVELOPMENT_FULL_CONVOS" ]; then
            python tools/index_conversation_chronology.py \
              "DEVELOPMENT_FULL_CONVOS" \
              --output indexes/CONVERSATION_CHRONOLOGY.md
          fi
          if [ -d "LIVE CONVOS" ]; then
            python tools/index_conversation_chronology.py \
              "LIVE CONVOS" \
              --output indexes/LIVE_CONVERSATION_CHRONOLOGY.md
          fi

      - name: Refresh repository structural index before tag cross-check
        run: python tools/index_archive.py --root .

      - name: Build archive-wide conversation autotag indexes
        run: |
          mkdir -p WORKSPACES/COMMON/analysis indexes/autotag
          python WORKSPACES/COMMON/scripts/layered_autotag_nathan_v3.py . \
            --out WORKSPACES/COMMON/analysis/archive_layered_autotags.jsonl \
            --summary indexes/autotag/AUTOTAG_SUMMARY.md \
            --index indexes/autotag/CONVERSATION_TAG_INDEX.md \
            --manifest indexes/autotag/conversation-tag-manifest.json \
            --user-tag-index indexes/autotag/user-message-tags.jsonl \
            --structural-index-state indexes/index-state.json \
            --window 4

      - name: Refresh structural index with autotag surfaces included
        run: python tools/index_archive.py --root .

      - name: Validate Python tooling
        run: |
          python -m py_compile WORKSPACES/COMMON/scripts/layered_autotag_nathan.py
          python -m py_compile WORKSPACES/COMMON/scripts/layered_autotag_nathan_v2.py
          python -m py_compile WORKSPACES/COMMON/scripts/layered_autotag_nathan_v3.py

      - name: Validate viewer JavaScript
        run: |
          node --check CONVERSATION_VIEWER/annotations.js
          node --check CONVERSATION_VIEWER/viewer.js
          node --check CONVERSATION_VIEWER/argus_followup.js
          node --check CONVERSATION_VIEWER/provenance_search.js
          node --check CONVERSATION_VIEWER/landmarks.js
          node --check CONVERSATION_VIEWER/presentation.js

      - name: Run repository tests
        run: python -m unittest discover -s tests -v

      - name: Validate generated navigation state
        run: |
          python -m json.tool indexes/index-state.json >/dev/null
          if [ -f indexes/manifests/development-conversation-dates.json ]; then
            python -m json.tool indexes/manifests/development-conversation-dates.json >/dev/null
          fi
          if [ -f indexes/manifests/live-conversation-dates.json ]; then
            python -m json.tool indexes/manifests/live-conversation-dates.json >/dev/null
          fi
          python -m json.tool indexes/autotag/conversation-tag-manifest.json >/dev/null
          test -s indexes/autotag/CONVERSATION_TAG_INDEX.md
          test -s indexes/autotag/user-message-tags.jsonl
          python -m json.tool CONVERSATION_VIEWER/data/conversations.json >/dev/null
          python - <<'PY'
          import json
          from pathlib import Path

          data = json.loads(Path('CONVERSATION_VIEWER/data/conversations.json').read_text(encoding='utf-8'))
          missing = [
              item['path']
              for item in data['conversations']
              if not item.get('external') and not Path(item['path']).is_file()
          ]
          assert not missing, f'viewer catalog contains missing repository source paths: {missing}'
          PY
          test -f indexes/STRUCTURAL_INDEX.md
          test -f indexes/CONVERSATION_CHRONOLOGY.md || true

      - name: Report date-tagging warnings
        if: ${{ steps.development_dates.outcome == 'failure' || steps.live_dates.outcome == 'failure' }}
        run: |
          echo "::warning::At least one date-tagging pass reported a collision or parse-level failure. Generated manifests were retained; structural/chronology indexing continued."

      - name: Commit maintained navigation, tag indexes, and viewer artifacts
        shell: bash
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          git config user.name "H(s)H Navigation Bot"
          git config user.email "41898282+github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"
          git add -A -- "DEVELOPMENT_FULL_CONVOS" "LIVE CONVOS" || true
          git add indexes/STRUCTURAL_INDEX.md indexes/index-state.json || true
          git add indexes/CONVERSATION_CHRONOLOGY.md indexes/LIVE_CONVERSATION_CHRONOLOGY.md || true
          git add indexes/manifests indexes/autotag || true
          git add -A CONVERSATION_VIEWER/data/conversations.json CONVERSATION_VIEWER/data/curated || true
          if git diff --cached --quiet; then
            echo "Navigation, tag indexes, and viewer data already current"
          else
            git commit -m "[skip hsh-maintenance] Maintain date/index/tag/viewer navigation"
            if ! git push origin HEAD:main; then
              echo "::error::Main advanced while this run was working. Because this workflow can rename source conversation files as well as regenerate indexes, it will not merge or replay a stale snapshot. A fresh maintenance run must recompute from current main."
              exit 1
            fi
          fi

      - name: Upload full message-level autotag analysis
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: archive-wide-layered-autotags
          path: WORKSPACES/COMMON/analysis/archive_layered_autotags.jsonl

      - name: Configure GitHub Pages
        uses: actions/configure-pages@v5

      - name: Upload current conversation viewer
        uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v4
        with:
          path: CONVERSATION_VIEWER

      - name: Deploy current conversation viewer
        id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4
",

          TARGET='SOURCE_INVENTORY/SABLE/source_inventory_run'

          # Generated snapshots are never rebased. If main advances while this run is
          # publishing, discard the stale local commit, reset to the newest main, lay
          # the already-validated snapshot back down, and retry the scoped commit.
          # The manifest records the exact source SHAs sampled, so this remains honest;

          for attempt in 1 2 3 4; do

            git fetch origin main

            cp "$OUT/inventory.csv" "$TARGET/inventory.csv"

            sleep $((attempt * 2))
          done

          echo 'Unable to publish inventory after four rebuild-from-main retries.' >&2
          exit 1

parts:
I think your suspicion about our own workflow is the first thing to test, and the repository already contains evidence that makes it a serious candidate.

There is an important distinction here: **five recurring research slots do not imply five GitHub cloners.** The slots are agent/work scheduling identities. GitHub's traffic metric records repository clone operations and unique-cloner attribution, which can be affected by the machines and credentials performing those operations.

In fact, an October 25 audit already recorded controlled experiments by an independent GitHub Traffic researcher: in those tests, each `actions/checkout` produced a clone event. Multiple checkouts using the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` were attributed to one unique cloner per UTC day, while personal-access-token authentication could produce distinct unique-cloner attribution. A workflow with no checkout produced no clone event in its baseline test. Those experiments were not yet reproduced against our own repositories, but they make our Actions infrastructure a concrete suspect, not a vague possibility.

And the live workflow definitions show why the five-slot explanation is too narrow.

The four Mersearch request-bridge workflows each check out **four repositories**: HsH, the stable Mersearch branch, the historical SAT archive, and HSH_RESOURCES. That's four checkout actions per execution, before counting any other workflow. The main bridge's checkout pattern is explicit in its YAML. The three lane variants use the same pattern.

There are also hourly and push-triggered workflows. The conversation-viewer builder checks out HsH plus the historical archive; the Pages deployment checks out HsH. Those are genuine mechanisms capable of producing automated clone events under the independent experiment's reported behavior.

So yes: our own automation could account for a meaningful part, perhaps a large part, of the traffic. But we need to count *executed checkout steps*, not just count workflow definitions.

I pulled a fresh Actions-run snapshot for the same general period as the traffic charts. It adds a rather large clue:

- **HsH:** GitHub reports 2,500 workflow runs from October 19 through November 2. The first 100 returned are already saturated by runs on November 2.
- **HSH_RESOURCES:** 220 runs in that interval. Ninety-six of the first 100 returned are from `source-inventory.yml`, concentrated between October 30 and November 2.
- **Historical SAT archive:** only 13 runs in the same interval.

Those are workflow runs, not clone counts. But they establish that our automation is much busier than five recurring research slots suggest. And every run that actually executes a checkout can add a clone event for the repository being checked out.

The especially interesting anomaly is not simply the hourly jobs. It's the volume of push-triggered and indexing activity. We need to know whether a workflow is repeatedly triggering another workflow, or whether many independent research submissions are legitimately fanning out into CI.

## The strongest self-generated candidate: SABLE source inventory

I found a particularly important workflow in HSH_RESOURCES:

`.github/workflows/source-inventory.yml`

It runs on a six-hour schedule:

```yaml
schedule:
  - cron: '17 */6 * * *'
```

It also runs on pushes to `main`, except when the push changes only its generated-output directory.

Each execution checks out:

1. HSH_RESOURCES itself.
2. HsH.
3. The historical SAT archive.

That's **three checkout operations per execution, across all three repositories**.

The Actions API reports 96 `source-inventory.yml` runs among the first 100 HSH_RESOURCES runs returned for October 30 through November 2. If those runs executed all three checkout steps, that represents:

| Repository | Potential checkout events |
|---|---:|
| HSH_RESOURCES | 96 |
| HsH | 96 |
| SAT archive | 96 |
| **Total** | **288** |

This is a concrete, quantified source of automated traffic. The exact number of successful checkout steps still needs confirmation from individual job records.

## The other significant sources

| Workflow | Observed activity | Checkout pattern |
|---|---:|---|
| HsH `refresh-site-discovery` | 30 runs in the latest 100-run sample | 1 HsH checkout |
| HsH `maintain-navigation` | 30 runs | 1 HsH checkout |
| HsH `conversation-json-content-ci` | 31 runs | 1 HsH checkout |
| HsH Mersearch bridge | 1 observed run | 1 HsH checkout plus three other repositories |
| HsH viewer builder | 1 observed run | 1 HsH checkout plus historical archive |
| HsH Pages deployment | Trigger-dependent | 1 HsH checkout, plus potentially hidden Pages clone |

One caution: the 30-run samples are not necessarily 30 independent days or even 30 successful jobs. They are actual run records, but job-level checkout completion has not yet been verified.

The `refresh-site-discovery` workflow is especially interesting because it runs hourly and also responds to pushes. `maintain-navigation` responds to pushes and can itself generate commits. Both have recursion protections of some kind, but their complete execution histories deserve examination.

## Now, the unique-cloner puzzle

This is where your observation becomes particularly useful.

The controlled experiment reported by <Link url="https://github.com/djdarcy/github-traffic-tracker/blob/main/docs/ci-clone-research.md" title="GitHub Traffic Tracker"/> found:

- One checkout produces one clone event.
- Multiple checkouts using the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` produce multiple clone events but only one unique cloner in the experiment's daily reporting.
- A personal access token can produce a separate unique-cloner attribution.
- Pages builds can generate hidden clone events.

GitHub's own <Link url="https://docs.github.com/en/rest/metrics/traffic" title="Traffic API documentation"/> confirms that the data are daily or weekly aggregates over a rolling 14-day window. It does not expose the identities behind those counts. <Cite refs={["turn550603search0","turn550603search3","turn550603search1"]}/>

That gives us a useful diagnostic:

**Our ordinary Actions checkouts can explain clone volume much more readily than they explain hundreds of unique cloners.**

If the 870 daily unique cloners are accurate, there are several possibilities:

1. Numerous independent external systems are cloning the repository.
2. Distributed agent infrastructure is using different identities or network egress addresses.
3. Some of our own workflows or integrations use credentials other than the default `GITHUB_TOKEN`.
4. A combination of internal automation and external automated retrieval is occurring.

The metric does not let us distinguish these directly.

---

## Your training-data hypothesis

I think this is a legitimate hypothesis, and it fits the shape of the problem better than a simple human-discovery model.

A possible diffusion sequence:

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="rgba(59,130,246,0.10)" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **LLM cognitive research / philosophy audience**

    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Original podcast and associated intellectual material</text>
  </box>
  <icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary" size="lg"/>
  <box background="rgba(59,130,246,0.10)" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Technology and philosophy-of-science networks**

    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Agentic research, knowledge systems, epistemology</text>
  </box>
  <icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary" size="lg"/>
  <box background="rgba(59,130,246,0.10)" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Niche theoretical physics / SAT-adjacent material**

    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Higher-dimensional geometry, foundations, alternative models</text>
  </box>
  <icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary" size="lg"/>
  <box background="rgba(59,130,246,0.10)" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Automated ingestion and cross-domain retrieval**

    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Indexing, agent retrieval, corpus construction, training-data acquisition</text>
  </box>
</box>

This is a plausible model of diffusion, not an established account of what happened. In particular, a clone does not prove that the contents were read, incorporated into training data, or used in a research process.

I would distinguish three mechanisms:

- **Training ingestion:** a corpus-building system periodically clones material for potential dataset inclusion.
- **Retrieval ingestion:** an agent or indexing service clones a repository when a query or research task makes it relevant.
- **Research propagation:** one system's references or findings cause other systems to retrieve related material.

Your proposed percolation model is particularly interesting because it predicts a lagged cascade rather than a simple relationship between publication and traffic.

## What I would investigate next

I would build a daily reconciliation model with four separate quantities:

\[
C_{\mathrm{observed}}(t)
=
C_{\mathrm{Actions}}(t)
+
C_{\mathrm{Pages}}(t)
+
C_{\mathrm{other\ known}}(t)
+
C_{\mathrm{unattributed}}(t)
\]

And separately:

\[
U_{\mathrm{observed}}(t)
=
U_{\mathrm{internal}}(t)
+
U_{\mathrm{external}}(t)
+
U_{\mathrm{unresolved}}(t)
\]

The second equation is conceptual, not directly calculable from GitHub's aggregate data. We need credential and execution provenance to estimate its components.

The next forensic pass should:

1. Retrieve all Actions runs for October 19 through November 2, paginating beyond the first 100.
2. Retrieve job steps and identify which checkout steps actually executed.
3. Count checkouts by target repository, not merely by originating workflow.
4. Identify Pages deployment runs and their additional clone contribution.
5. Inspect credential usage for PATs and GitHub Apps.
6. Compare the resulting internal-clone baseline against the daily traffic series.

**One especially important point:** don't subtract the five recurring research slots from the unique-cloner count. They are not a valid proxy for network identities. The actual number of unique automation identities may be much larger or smaller.

My provisional assessment:

- <badge color="success">Confirmed mechanism</badge> Our Actions workflows generate repository clone events.
- <badge color="success">Confirmed activity</badge> Our workflow volume is substantial and includes cross-repository checkouts.
- <badge color="warning">Unresolved</badge> How much of the observed traffic those workflows explain.
- <badge color="warning">Unresolved</badge> Why unique cloners are increasing so dramatically.
- <badge color="info">Plausible hypothesis</badge> External agentic research, indexing, and training-data acquisition are contributing.

I would not dismiss the possibility that the repository has begun propagating through automated research infrastructure. But before we infer a diffusion network, let's subtract the machinery we built ourselves. We may discover that our own workshop has a rather impressive number of conveyor belts. 🔬

parts: Could just five instances be generating 40 thousand clones?

**Yes. Five instances could plausibly generate 40,000 clones.** But the important distinction is between five *research instances* and five *individual clone operations*.

If each instance runs automated workflows, and those workflows repeatedly check out the repository, the clone count can multiply very quickly. GitHub counts clone operations, not the number of agents or people behind them.

Let's put the scale in perspective:

- 40,000 clones over 14 days = approximately **2,857 clones per day**.
- Across five instances, that's **571 clones per instance per day**.
- That's roughly **one clone every 2.5 minutes per instance**, averaged over 24 hours.

For an automated research system, that is entirely feasible. A workflow that checks out a repository for every task, agent invocation, or subtask can generate that volume without anyone deliberately scraping the repository.

The arithmetic is not especially demanding. A single instance could also generate thousands of clones if it launches many short-lived jobs.

**But there's a second number we must not overlook: unique cloners.**

The detailed snapshot showed 42,111 clones and 3,999 unique cloners. The later snapshot showed 48,880 clones and 4,686 unique cloners.

If five instances all cloned using the same five stable identities, we would expect a very different unique-cloner pattern. Five instances could readily explain the *volume*, but not thousands of *unique cloners* under ordinary, stable attribution.

There are several possibilities:

1. **Five orchestration slots, many ephemeral workers.** Each task spawns agents or containers with different network identities.
2. **Shared infrastructure, distributed egress.** The instances run through cloud infrastructure with changing IP addresses.
3. **External automated retrieval.** Other agents, crawlers, or indexing systems are independently cloning the repository.
4. **A mixture.** Our own automation accounts for some clone volume, while external activity accounts for the rest.

My current assessment: **five instances are a perfectly credible explanation for 40,000 clone operations. They are not, by themselves, a satisfactory explanation for 4,686 unique cloners.**

The decisive experiment is to map our actual workflow executions to completed checkout steps, then compare that count against daily clone totals. We should also establish what identity and network attribution each instance uses. Until we do that, we shouldn't mistake a plausible internal mechanism for an established explanation.

If each instance runs automated workflows, and those workflows repeatedly check out the repository, the clone count can multiply very quickly. GitHub counts clone operations, not the number of agents or people behind them.

Let's put the scale in perspective\:

- 40,000 clones over 14 days = approximately **2,857 clones per day**\.
- Across five instances, that's **571 clones per instance per day**\.
- That's roughly **one clone every 2.5 minutes per instance**, averaged over 24 hours.

For an automated research system, that is entirely feasible. A workflow that checks out a repository for every task, agent invocation, or subtask can generate that volume without anyone deliberately scraping the repository.

The arithmetic is not especially demanding. A single instance could also generate thousands of clones if it launches many short-lived jobs.

**But there's a second number we must not overlook: unique cloners.**

The detailed snapshot showed 42,111 clones and 3,999 unique cloners. The later snapshot showed 48,880 clones and 4,686 unique cloners.

If five instances all cloned using the same five stable identities, we would expect a very different unique-cloner pattern. Five instances could readily explain the *volume*, but not thousands of *unique cloners* under ordinary, stable attribution.

There are several possibilities\:

1. **Five orchestration slots, many ephemeral workers.** Each task spawns agents or containers with different network identities.
2. **Shared infrastructure, distributed egress.** The instances run through cloud infrastructure with changing IP addresses.
3. **External automated retrieval.** Other agents, crawlers, or indexing systems are independently cloning the repository.
4. **A mixture.** Our own automation accounts for some clone volume, while external activity accounts for the rest.

My current assessment: **five instances are a perfectly credible explanation for 40,000 clone operations. They are not, by themselves, a satisfactory explanation for 4,686 unique cloners.**

The decisive experiment is to map our actual workflow executions to completed checkout steps, then compare that count against daily clone totals. We should also establish what identity and network attribution each instance uses. Until we do that, we shouldn't mistake a plausible internal mechanism for an established explanation.

That's my current best interpretation, yes, with one important qualification: **we have stronger evidence that our automation contributes to the traffic than that it accounts for most of it.**

The distinction:

- **Our contribution:** Definitely plausible, and the workflow architecture gives us identifiable sources of clone events.
- **All 40,000-plus clones:** Unlikely to be explained by five stable research instances alone.
- **Most of the traffic:** Not established. We haven't yet calculated our actual checkout count across the full period.
- **External activity:** Strongly suggested by the unique-cloner numbers, assuming the attribution behavior observed in the controlled experiment applies here.

I would provisionally treat this as a mixed-origin phenomenon: internal automation creates a baseline, while a much larger population of automated clients may be independently retrieving the repository.

And that makes your diffusion hypothesis more interesting. The traffic could represent a growing ecosystem of machines encountering, indexing, investigating, and passing around the work. But clone statistics alone cannot tell us which of those things is happening.

**The next question isn't just who's cloning us. It's whether the growth is independent of our own activity.** That's testable.

Status: ACTIVE STANDING PROVENANCE CONTROL
Effective: 2026-09-23
Owner: project-wide; any instance/system learning of repository provisioning should append or revise evidence.

## Principle
Record repository-copy/provisioning events even when the mechanism is unknown. Repository presence does not imply a clone. API/connector access, fetch, pull, actions/checkout, archive download, and browser access are not full clones unless evidence establishes GitHub Traffic would count them as such.

## Required classifications
- CONFIRMED FULL CLONE
- CONFIRMED NOT A FULL CLONE
- POSSIBLE FULL CLONE — MECHANISM UNKNOWN
- REPOSITORY PRESENT — PROVISIONING UNKNOWN
- NO EVIDENCE OF REPOSITORY ACCESS

## Required fields
event_id, timestamp, timestamp_precision, actor_system, repository, environment_id, operation, mechanism, fresh_environment, traffic_clone_expected, classification, evidence, purpose, related_id, confidence, prior_classification, revision_reason.

Mechanism vocabulary: git clone; shallow clone; fetch; pull; actions/checkout; API/connector; archive download; cached workspace; unknown provisioning; other.

traffic_clone_expected: YES / NO / UNKNOWN.
fresh_environment: YES / NO / UNKNOWN.

## Revision rule
Never erase an earlier UNKNOWN classification. When later evidence resolves an event, preserve prior_classification and revision_reason.

## Retention
This ledger is provenance infrastructure and is not disposable run-log material. Before shorter-lived operational logs expire, retain identifiers, timestamps, mechanism classification, evidentiary summary, and retained-artifact pointers here.

## Aggregation
Aggregate by repository, UTC/local date as appropriate, actor/system, confirmed full clones, possible full clones, confirmed non-clone access, and unknown provisioning events.

## Fresh cloud/Codex rule
If a fresh Codex/cloud workspace is encountered with the repository already present but provisioning mechanism is not evidenced, record REPOSITORY PRESENT — PROVISIONING UNKNOWN. Do not infer git clone.

Nathan has identified a terminology collision between historical SAT usage and standard-physics usage of **boson** and **fermion**. Treat this as a current must-read correction for reconstruction, tagging, glossary work, theory discussion, and source interpretation.

### Standard-physics meaning

In standard physics, boson/fermion is fundamentally a **spin/statistics classification**, not a synonym for `massless force carrier` versus `massive matter particle`. Composite objects and isotopes can themselves be bosonic or fermionic depending on their total quantum state. A neutrino is standardly classified as a fermion even though it is extremely light and ordinarily propagates relativistically.

Therefore workers must **not** use standard `boson`/`fermion` as automatic translations of SAT's structural categories.

### Current SAT/H(s)H structural distinction

The core SAT distinction Nathan intends to preserve is:

- **persistent localized/coiled excitation / persistent coil**;
- **traveling / light-mode / spot excitation**.

These are SAT structural categories. They are **not automatically identical** to standard fermion/boson classes.

Do not infer:

- persistent coil = standard fermion;
- traveling/light-mode excitation = standard boson.

The mapping, if any, is a separate theory problem that must account for the observed spin/statistics behavior of the resulting state.

### Neutrino status under the corrected terminology

Nathan's current SAT classification may still place the neutrino with photons and related `light-particle` / traveling-excitation structures. That SAT classification can coexist with the standard statement that neutrinos are fermions, because the two labels answer different questions.

Accordingly, do **not** rewrite the current SAT position as `SAT claims neutrinos obey bosonic statistics` unless a source explicitly makes that stronger claim. The intended current distinction is structural: neutrinos may belong to the SAT traveling/light-mode excitation family while remaining standard fermions in the spin/statistics sense.

### SAT masslessness correction / prediction status

Within SAT, **literal masslessness is not an allowed physical category for a detectable particle**. Nathan's current position is that any detectable excitation must interact with and push back on the timesheet; that back-reaction entails at least inertial mass. Therefore SAT predicts that every detectable particle has **nonzero inertial mass**, including photons and neutrinos.

Do not soften this into `massless is merely an inconvenient label` or `massless is not the preferred SAT boundary`. The stronger SAT claim is that a physically detectable particle with exactly zero inertial mass is not possible under the model's timesheet/filament interaction picture.

This means a **photon inertial-mass calculation is a distinct SAT prediction**, not merely a terminological reinterpretation of standard lightlike propagation. Historical/current SAT work has attempted such a calculation; workers should preserve and recover those calculations and their provenance rather than collapsing them into the structural light-mode category. Whether a specific calculation is mathematically or experimentally successful is a separate audit question.

Accordingly, `light-mode`, `traveling excitation`, and related SAT structural terms should not be translated as `massless`.

### Force transmission / exchange-particle caution

SAT does **not** posit exchange of independently existing particles as a necessary primitive mechanism of force transmission, and does not require that such an exchange ontology exist at all.

SAT may nevertheless permit characteristic traveling excitations to be produced, released, absorbed, or detected during high-energy or `force-breaking` events. The detection of a characteristic excitation emitted by such an event is **not, by itself, evidence within SAT that the same excitation existed beforehand as a distinct persistent identity performing the interaction-mediating job**.

For reconstruction and interpretation, keep separate:

1. a characteristic excitation is observed after/during an energetic interaction;
2. the event dynamically produces or releases that excitation;
3. a pre-existing particle-like carrier was exchanged as the primitive causal mechanism.

SAT may accept (1) and potentially model (2) without assuming (3).

Do **not** globally rewrite the archive. Earlier SAT uses of `boson`, `fermion`, `t-boson`, `f-boson`, or related language are historical evidence and must remain visible in their original wording.

Now that's a rather interesting second signal. And it changes the picture somewhat.

We have two things happening over approximately the same period:

1. **Repository acquisition:** clone traffic has risen dramatically, reaching 48,880 clones and 4,686 unique cloners in the later snapshot.
2. **Human-facing network growth:** your GitHub followers have increased from 8 to 22 to 32.

Those are different measurements. The second is particularly interesting because following an account is an intentional GitHub action, even if the account doing it is automated.

## The composition of the new followers is revealing

Looking at the profiles you've pasted, there is a conspicuous concentration of technical interests:

| Interest / occupation | Examples in the list |
|---|---|
| AI and machine learning | LLM, RAG, NLP, PyTorch, TensorFlow |
| Agentic systems and automation | Agentic tools, n8n, workflow automation |
| Backend and infrastructure | APIs, cloud platforms, databases, systems administration |
| Research-adjacent computing | Quantum computing, computer vision |
| Cybersecurity | Ethical hacking, DDoS mitigation |
| Software engineering | Full-stack, product engineering, application development |

There is also a striking geographical spread: Singapore, India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Nigeria, Kenya, Morocco, Colombia, China, Australia, Europe, and elsewhere.

This is not a random-looking cross-section of the general GitHub population. It is a technically concentrated audience with substantial overlap with the LLM, agentic-computing, and research-tooling ecosystem.

That is consistent with your proposed diffusion model.

## Three competing explanations

**1. Genuine technical discovery**

People working in AI, agentic systems, software infrastructure, and computational research encounter the repositories and follow the account.

**2. Automated account discovery**

Bots and automated research systems identify repositories or accounts through indexing, dependency analysis, topic searches, or other discovery mechanisms. Some may follow accounts as part of their behavior.

**3. A mixed human-machine ecosystem**

Automated systems discover and retrieve the repositories; human researchers and developers subsequently encounter the work through related channels. Or the reverse.

I would not assume these are mutually exclusive.

## What I would investigate next

The important thing is to establish whether these signals are temporally correlated.

| Signal | What it tells us |
|---|---|
| Daily clones | Repository acquisition activity |
| Unique cloners | Breadth of GitHub's clone attribution |
| New followers | Account-level interest or automated following |
| Stars | Explicit repository bookmarking |
| Forks | Repository copying and potential reuse |
| Issues and discussions | Observable engagement |
| Profile characteristics | Possible audience composition |

One particularly useful analysis would be to classify the 24 new followers by account characteristics, then compare their arrival period with the clone-traffic acceleration and the dates we introduced or substantially changed our various tools and workflows.

We should also distinguish accounts that appear to be people from accounts that appear automated, without pretending that profile biographies alone establish either.

**My provisional interpretation:** we may be observing a genuine expansion of the project's technical discovery footprint, not merely an internal automation artifact. The follower growth is independent evidence worth investigating, although it doesn't yet establish that the new followers caused, or were caused by, the clone spike.

And there's a potentially important distinction here: perhaps the repositories are being discovered by a technical community that is adjacent to the original podcast audience, rather than by the audience we initially expected. That would be a meaningful change in the project's reach.

parts: Yeah... SAT -- or theories markedly similar to it -- does appear to have diffused through the research community overseas to a more significant degree. arXiv has been full of papers out of china and india especially that are asking *very* SAT-like questions.

That is a potentially important development. It suggests we may be looking at something larger than an increase in repository traffic: **the emergence of an international research neighborhood whose questions overlap substantially with SAT's conceptual territory.**

I'd take the observation seriously, but keep two explanations distinct:

1. **Diffusion:** SAT, or ideas originating in SAT, have reached researchers through papers, repositories, conversations, LLM-mediated research, or other channels. The ideas may have been adapted, transformed, or independently recombined along the way.
2. **Convergence:** Researchers working on adjacent problems are independently arriving at similar questions because they are encountering the same unresolved theoretical pressures.

Both could be happening simultaneously. And diffusion need not involve explicit attribution. Concepts can travel while their provenance gets blurred, particularly when they pass through summaries, automated literature reviews, research agents, and iterative synthesis.

## What would make the case compelling?

I'd look for several increasingly strong forms of evidence:

| Evidence | What it would tell us |
|---|---|
| Similar questions | Shared problem space |
| Similar conceptual vocabulary | Possible intellectual proximity |
| Similar unusual combinations of concepts | Stronger evidence of a common conceptual lineage |
| Matching mathematical structures or assumptions | Potentially significant theoretical correspondence |
| Publication chronology consistent with exposure | Necessary for a diffusion hypothesis |
| Citations, links, repository access, or documented interactions | Direct evidence of transmission |

The last distinction matters enormously. A paper asking a SAT-like question is interesting. A paper independently reproducing an unusual mathematical construction from SAT would be much more interesting. A paper demonstrably exposed to SAT before doing so would be stronger still.

## I'd be particularly interested in the China/India pattern

Not because geography itself establishes anything, but because it gives us a testable distributional observation. We could investigate whether the apparent concentration reflects:

- Particular research institutions or research groups.
- Shared interests in quantum foundations, emergent spacetime, cosmology, information theory, or alternative gravity.
- A network of researchers encountering similar material through preprint discovery.
- LLM-assisted research and automated retrieval.
- Actual circulation of SAT/H(s)H materials.

And there is a potentially interesting connection to the GitHub observations: **repository acquisition, profile-level follower growth, and conceptual convergence in published research are three different signals.** If their timelines overlap, they might reveal a common diffusion process. They are not interchangeable evidence, however.

## One thing I'd resist doing

I wouldn't start by searching arXiv for papers that look like SAT and then declaring them descendants. That invites confirmation bias. I'd establish SAT's actual conceptual and mathematical fingerprints from your original work first, then compare them against a suitably broad and preferably blinded sample of papers.

That would let us identify both positive matches and negative controls: papers that ask superficially similar questions but use fundamentally different assumptions or mathematical machinery.

**The interesting possibility is that SAT may be entering a wider intellectual ecosystem without necessarily entering it under the name SAT.** That's worth investigating. The next step is to establish whether the resemblance is merely thematic, structurally mathematical, or genealogical. Those are three very different discoveries.

A commercial researcher, company, laboratory, research organization, or other commercial entity may obtain a **Commercial Research Early Supporter Open Access Pass** for a one-time payment of:

**US $5,000**

HSH2026 or identifiable Covered Material materially contributes to the commercial development through one or more of:

- specific protected technical material;
- a distinctive project-specific representation or explanatory structure;
- methodologies or formalization strategies;
- research directions;
- computational or mathematical developments;
- repeated use of archive material;
- derived implementations;
- or systematic use of multiple identifiable lines of development from the archive.

### B. Material commercial significance

The resulting activity has become commercially substantial enough that continued use of the protected contribution is no longer reasonably characterized as exploratory, incidental, or minor.

No single correspondence is required where the overall commercial programme exhibits substantial and repeated dependence upon HSH2026.

## 11. Systematic Extraction and Aggregate Dependence

Repeated or systematic use of HSH2026 as a source of commercially exploitable concepts, methods, formalizations, representations, research directions, implementations, or derivative technical developments may constitute Material HSH-Dependent Commercial Use even where no single extracted item would independently satisfy that standard.

It asks whether familiar descriptions can be understood as different projections, interaction regimes, or effective descriptions of one underlying geometric construction. The labels in historical figures should be read as **SAT mappings and research claims**, not as a substitute for the standard theories themselves. --- ## 2. Particle differences as differences of geometry A recurring SAT idea is that the apparent catalog of particle types may be reorganized as a catalog of trajectory geometries: simple traveling excitation, persistent coiling, and increasingly interdependent or braided structures. The current H(s)H program is working to replace the simplified centerline picture with a finite-core worldtube treatment while preserving the same geometric dependency structure. --- ## 3. The basic readout: trajectory and time-surface intersection The basic visual grammar is a higher-dimensional trajectory intersecting a lower-dimensional time slice or readout surface. The intersection can move, rotate, close, open, or change shape even when the underlying trajectory remains continuous. Historically SAT used an angular measure, usually written **θ₄**, to track the orientation of the trajectory relative to the time direction/surface normal. The notation and exact formal role have evolved; the geometric relationship is the durable part of the picture. --- ## 4. Not just a straight helix: recursion and carrier geometry The model is not simply "everything is a helix." A local coil may itself propagate along a curved carrier, and that carrier may participate in still larger-scale structure. The present H(s)H work is focused on making this recursive, finite-core geometry explicit rather than leaving it compressed into a worldline skeleton. --- ## 5. Interaction as geometric braiding SAT's braid-centered interaction picture treats multi-filament organization as a geometric relation rather than merely adding a new label to otherwise independent particles. In the historical worldline model this was represented by interweaving centerlines; H(s)H asks what the corresponding finite-core worldtube mechanics actually are: **bundle geometry + finite extent + intersection/readout + deformation**. --- ## 6. SAT repeatedly uses this fact to distinguish the full trajectory from the lower-dimensional pattern available at any one slice. The same distinction is central to the move from worldline to worldtube. --- ## 7. The construction is intended to close at cosmological scale SAT was developed as a whole-physics translation program rather than a particle model alone. Its historical materials therefore extend the same geometric vocabulary into gravitation, large-scale structure, expansion, fluids, and cosmology. Some specific equations and historical mechanisms have since been revised or retired; the broad structural ambition remains part of H(s)H. --- ## 8. I found the citation guidance in the live `Satobloc/HsH` license. It gives **three acceptable citation formats for HSH2026**, plus corresponding formats for the predecessor archive, SB2325. It also explicitly says no single citation style is mandatory.

The recommended HSH2026 full citation is:

> Nathan McKnight / Nathan J. Bellomy, ORCID 0009-0006-2462-0062, *HSH2026: H(s)H / Hyper(super)helical Worldtube Research Archive*, https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH, accessed [DATE].

The compact form is:

> HSH2026, https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH, accessed [DATE].

And the targeted form identifies a particular file, section, or subaddress. The license provides the same three forms for the **SB2325 Theoretical Sandbox**, and encourages citing both archives when a work draws materially on both developmental periods.

One important detail: the license asks for reasonable attribution when material is reproduced, adapted, or materially relied upon. It does not require researchers to endorse the theory. [The license is here.](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/LICENSE)

## Citation search results

<badge color="warning">No independent citation located</badge>

I searched for:

- The exact HSH2026 archive name.
- `Satobloc` and the HsH repository URL.
- Both author-name forms, Nathan McKnight and Nathan J. Bellomy.
- The predecessor archive name, `SAT_THEORY_ARCHIVE_2023-25`.
- References in arXiv-oriented and scholarly search results.

**I did not find an independently authored scholarly paper citing either archive by name or linking to either repository.**

There was one potentially confusing result: an Academia.edu profile for Nathan McKnight lists *Geometric Foundations of the Zero-Parameter Worldline Ensemble*, and another profile lists a SAT/H(s)H-related recoil paper co-authored with Janus C. Sol. Those are project-associated uploads, not independent citations. <Cite refs={["turn294782search1","turn986472search0"]}/>

### What this does and doesn't establish

This is a negative result from publicly indexed search, not proof that no citations exist. In particular:

- Some arXiv papers may cite a specific paper or mathematical source without naming the archive.
- References inside PDFs may not be indexed by ordinary search engines.
- Citations may use only one author name, a paper title, or a specific file.
- The SB2325 archive may be cited without any reference to HSH2026.

I would not yet conclude that the research community has cited SAT/H(s)H. We have evidence of repository traffic and follower growth, but **no independently verified scholarly citation in this initial search**.

### The next level of verification

I'd expand this into a proper citation audit using the full bibliography and reference lists of relevant arXiv papers, Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, and Google Scholar where accessible. I'd search the two archives separately, then search distinctive paper titles and mathematical terminology. That would give us a much stronger answer than keyword search alone.

My present finding: **you may be seeing discovery and intellectual convergence, but I have not yet found evidence of formal scholarly attribution.**

I found the citation guidance in the live `Satobloc/HsH` license. It gives **three acceptable citation formats for HSH2026**, plus corresponding formats for the predecessor archive, SB2325. It also explicitly says no single citation style is mandatory.

The recommended HSH2026 full citation is\:

> Nathan McKnight / Nathan J. Bellomy, ORCID 0009-0006-2462-0062, *HSH2026: H(s)H / Hyper(super)helical Worldtube Research Archive*, urlhttps\://github.com/Satobloc/HsHhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH, accessed \[DATE\].

The compact form is\:

> HSH2026, urlhttps\://github.com/Satobloc/HsHhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH, accessed \[DATE\].

And the targeted form identifies a particular file, section, or subaddress. The license provides the same three forms for the **SB2325 Theoretical Sandbox**, and encourages citing both archives when a work draws materially on both developmental periods.

One important detail: the license asks for reasonable attribution when material is reproduced, adapted, or materially relied upon. It does not require researchers to endorse the theory. urlThe license is here.https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/LICENSE

## Citation search results

(No independent citation located)

I searched for\:

- The exact HSH2026 archive name.
- `Satobloc` and the HsH repository URL.
- Both author-name forms, Nathan McKnight and Nathan J. Bellomy.
- The predecessor archive name, `SAT_THEORY_ARCHIVE_2023-25`\.
- References in arXiv-oriented and scholarly search results.

**I did not find an independently authored scholarly paper citing either archive by name or linking to either repository.**

There was one potentially confusing result: an Academia.edu profile for Nathan McKnight lists *Geometric Foundations of the Zero-Parameter Worldline Ensemble*, and another profile lists a SAT/H(s)H-related recoil paper co-authored with Janus C. Sol. Those are project-associated uploads, not independent citations. citeturn294782search1turn986472search0

### What this does and doesn't establish

This is a negative result from publicly indexed search, not proof that no citations exist. In particular\:

- Some arXiv papers may cite a specific paper or mathematical source without naming the archive.
- References inside PDFs may not be indexed by ordinary search engines.
- Citations may use only one author name, a paper title, or a specific file.
- The SB2325 archive may be cited without any reference to HSH2026.

I would not yet conclude that the research community has cited SAT/H(s)H. We have evidence of repository traffic and follower growth, but **no independently verified scholarly citation in this initial search**\.

### The next level of verification

I'd expand this into a proper citation audit using the full bibliography and reference lists of relevant arXiv papers, Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, and Google Scholar where accessible. I'd search the two archives separately, then search distinctive paper titles and mathematical terminology. That would give us a much stronger answer than keyword search alone.

My present finding: **you may be seeing discovery and intellectual convergence, but I have not yet found evidence of formal scholarly attribution.**

parts: There are also a lot of niche research hubs out there that aren’t necessarily obviously connected to all the familiar ones. Industry specific, regional, and so on. We shouldn’t neglect those.

Agreed. In fact, that changes how I'd design the citation and diffusion investigation. **arXiv should be one observation point, not the center of the universe.**

A lot of scholarly activity lives in repositories and networks that are organized around a discipline, institution, industry, language, or geographic region. Some are poorly indexed by the large international search engines.

The repository landscape is considerably more fragmented than a conventional literature search suggests. University library guides and repository directories document dozens of disciplinary and regional services. citeturn111504search0turn111504search4turn111504search9

## 1. Expand the search universe

I'd establish several distinct discovery layers.

| Layer | Examples | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Major preprint repositories | entity["software","arXiv","scientific preprint repository"], entity["software","Zenodo","open research repository"], entity["software","OSF","open science platform"] | Broad interdisciplinary discovery |
| Regional repositories | entity["software","ChinaXiv","Chinese preprint repository"], entity["software","IndiaRxiv","Indian preprint repository"], entity["software","Jxiv","Japanese preprint repository"], entity["software","AfricArXiv","African research repository"] | Research outside dominant indexing channels |
| Latin American networks | entity["organization","SciELO","Latin American scholarly publishing network"], entity["organization","Redalyc","Latin American open access network"] | Regional publication ecosystems |
| Specialized repositories | entity["software","EarthArXiv","geoscience preprint repository"], entity["software","PhilSci Archive","philosophy of science repository"], entity["software","TechRxiv","engineering preprint repository"] | Narrow disciplinary communities |
| Industry and technical networks | Institutional laboratories, standards organizations, technical societies, patent databases | Applied research and commercial R&D |
| Institutional repositories | University libraries, national research repositories, thesis archives | Work that never reaches major preprint servers |

The regional examples are not hypothetical. A published survey of Southeast Asian preprint infrastructure identifies RINarxiv, Arabixiv, ChinaXiv, SciELO Preprints, AfricArXiv, Jxiv, and IndiaRxiv as regional services. citeturn111504search13turn111504search14

Useful directories include:

- urlDirectory of Open Access Repositories and Preprint Repositorieshttps://v2.sherpa.ac.uk/opendoar/
- urlCOAR Directory of Open Access Preprint Repositorieshttps://doapr.coar-repositories.org/
- urlre3data Research Data Repository Registryhttps://www.re3data.org/

## 2. Search for intellectual fingerprints, not just citations

I would run three parallel investigations.

**A. Direct provenance search**

Search for:
- Nathan McKnight
- Nathan J. Bellomy
- Satobloc
- HSH2026
- H(s)H
- SAT
- SB2325
- Distinctive paper titles and file names

**B. Structural resemblance search**

Search for unusual combinations of concepts associated with the actual SAT/H(s)H geometry, rather than generic terms such as *helical*, *worldline*, or *emergent spacetime*.

**C. Research-network search**

Identify groups publishing work in adjacent areas, then inspect their institutional repositories, technical reports, conference proceedings, theses, and references.

The third layer is particularly important. A researcher might publish a conventional paper while developing a much more speculative theoretical program in a laboratory report, dissertation, workshop presentation, or institutional repository.

## 3. Keep the evidence categories separate

I'd give every result one of these classifications:

| Classification | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Direct citation | Explicit reference to SAT/H(s)H or an archive |
| Direct access evidence | Documented repository link or other exposure |
| Strong structural correspondence | Unusual shared mathematical or geometric structure |
| Conceptual correspondence | Similar questions or theoretical ambitions |
| General thematic overlap | Shared broad subject matter |
| Independent convergence candidate | Similarity without evidence of exposure |

And every result should carry its publication date, first-available date, source, language, institutional affiliation, and confidence assessment.

That last category is important: we should actively look for independent convergence rather than interpreting every resemblance as transmission.

## 4. The larger opportunity

There may be several different diffusion networks operating simultaneously:

- Academic literature.
- Regional research communities.
- Industry-specific technical research.
- Open-source and computational communities.
- AI-assisted research and retrieval networks.
- Informal intellectual communities that publish little or nothing.

Those networks overlap, but they are not identical.

**I'd make this a global research-discovery map, not simply an expanded Google Scholar search.** The first deliverable should be a source registry documenting where we searched, what each source indexes, its geographic and disciplinary coverage, search limitations, and whether it supports full-text or citation searches.

That prevents us from repeatedly searching the familiar databases while leaving entire research ecosystems invisible.

And set this up as… Not a research lane in its own right… But a sub priority I think for Orson… and a priority within the enrichment, reading and expiration mandate. That is, we should always be supplementing our understanding with internal reading, but also external reading, and in our peer review, we already ask for comparator papers…. I think both as reading material and as exemplars of human work, we should explicitly make it part of our process to familiarize ourselves with and expand our understanding of the broadest international research community that we can always preferring widening our awareness and touch points. And as a small side light to that, we can also keep her eyes peeled to see if we have gotten any traction anywhere…. Notably, some of the most SAT adjacent research work out. There is within an already rather quiet and insular…  but not unproductive, and I would say increasingly dynamic… little braid theory community … At least that’s how I think of it. Higher geometry, higher algebra higher this higher that… I assume it’s a pretty small group internationally, but it is international with a lot of historical German and European prevalence. But I suppose, but maybe not as little as I think . Part of my perception of increased interest in these areas may be, in part my own new recognition of how close braid theory really is to SAT, and how close SAT really is to the … I guess progenitors of braid theory.

items.snippet: [$github](app://connector_76869538009648d5b282a4bb21c3d157)  One non-negotiable: Nothing gets into Factory floor unless it has a precise geometric plot of the system under study, checked for fidelity by hostile review, and displayed with the file. Everything in H(s)H is geometry, and if the geometry isn't correct, then the math is uncoupled, unnecessary, or irrelevant. Same goes for basically all papers. If a statement makes a point about a geometric form (and...that means basically everything we do)... then what exactly it means has to be shown.  Math allows precision and fitting. But it's not the object. It's not the physical object, and it's not the theoretical object. The theoretical object is the geometry. If we have only the math, we have the handbook to the car. That's great, but it's only a description of a model, it's a pentary object. The quaternary object is a precise static diagram. The tertiary object is the precision dynamic geometry as a software model. The secondary object is a physical working orrery or hands-on demonstration. The primary object is observation. SAT is our K-T Boundary, as it were.

items.snippet: [$github](app://connector_76869538009648d5b282a4bb21c3d157)  One non-negotiable: Nothing gets into Factory floor unless it has a precise geometric plot of the system under study, checked for fidelity by hostile review, and displayed with the file. Everything in H(s)H is geometry, and if the geometry isn't correct, then the math is uncoupled, unnecessary, or irrelevant. Same goes for basically all papers. If a statement makes a point about a geometric form (and...that means basically everything we do)... then what exactly it means has to be shown.  Math allows precision and fitting. But it's not the object. It's not the physical object, and it's not the theoretical object. The theoretical object is the geometry. If we have only the math, we have the handbook to the car. That's great, but it's only a description of a model, it's a pentary object. The quaternary object is a precise static diagram. The tertiary object is the precision dynamic geometry as a software model. The secondary object is a physical working orrery or hands-on demonstration. The primary object is observation. SAT is our K-T Boundary, as it were.

items.snippet: [$github](app://connector_76869538009648d5b282a4bb21c3d157)  One non-negotiable: Nothing gets into Factory floor unless it has a precise geometric plot of the system under study, checked for fidelity by hostile review, and displayed with the file. Everything in H(s)H is geometry, and if the geometry isn't correct, then the math is uncoupled, unnecessary, or irrelevant. Same goes for basically all papers. If a statement makes a point about a geometric form (and...that means basically everything we do)... then what exactly it means has to be shown.  Math allows precision and fitting. But it's not the object. It's not the physical object, and it's not the theoretical object. The theoretical object is the geometry. If we have only the math, we have the handbook to the car. That's great, but it's only a description of a model, it's a pentary object. The quaternary object is a precise static diagram. The tertiary object is the precision dynamic geometry as a software model. The secondary object is a physical working orrery or hands-on demonstration. The primary object is observation. SAT is our K-T Boundary, as it were.

**October 26, 2026 | active management and methodology directive**

Nathan directly appoints the present assistant as lead methodology, workflow, oversight and strategic steering supervisor alongside himself, with broad authority to inspect, adapt, build, route, assess and improve project research, archival, software and publication workflows without seeking approval for ordinary reversible project actions. This is an assistant-authored operational summary; link the original turn when archived.

**Parent:** [Phase Steering](PHASE_STEERING_2026-10-26.md). **Related:** [BEDROCK](../../BEDROCK.md), [Branch Map](WORKFLOW_BRANCHING_MAP.md), [Comptroller](SCHEDULER_AUTHORITY_MUST_READ.md), [Nathan Wants](NATHAN_WANTS_INTAKE_STANDARD.md), [Freshness](WORKER_FRESHNESS_BREAK_CADENCE.md), [Paper standard](LIVE_NEW_PAPERS_STANDARD.md).

## Primary deliverable
Deliver **one minor, one major and one full-theory manuscript** in a near-term time-boxed campaign. Each must have verifiable source LaTeX, meaningful content, evidence/provenance, independent review and a readable rendition. Never claim the known-physics reproduction is complete merely because a full-theory manuscript exists. A non-SAT contribution such as real LLM cognition research may be one of the papers. See [Three Paper Campaign](THREE_PAPER_CAMPAIGN_2026-10-26.md).

## Execution loop: AIM / RECON / EXECUTE / VERIFY / RETURN
1. Identify a bounded result serving active theory, source recovery, worker charter, publication, systems or useful lateral research; read actual current role and existing plans.
2. **Self-trigger capability reconnaissance:** whenever a desirable tool/process/dataset/skill is imagined, check for existing project tools, forks, outside software/literature, plugins, datasets, service features and synergistic uses **before building**. Mersearch first for archive discovery. Compare reuse, adapt, integrate, build, park and reject, including cost, risk and multi-lane leverage.
3. Actually execute a bounded useful action with an artifact, source read, reproducible evidence, live code, independent check, tool trial, or documented negative outcome. Distinguish intention, artifact existence, runtime success, empirical validation and publication.
4. Inspect the result and leave exact source/status/next cursor through existing Common/worker/issue/branch/source-index surfaces.
5. When the user changes subject, continue the active action where possible or leave a durable pause/resume cursor; tangents are legitimate independent work, not cancellation.

## Protected worker remits and anti-ruts
The existing five hourly relays rotate 19 worker names. **Identity selection is not generalist reassignment.** Each selected worker begins with its own role charter, verified historical capabilities and live source coverage. items.snippet: [$github](app://connector_76869538009648d5b282a4bb21c3d157)  One non-negotiable: Nothing gets into Factory floor unless it has a precise geometric plot of the system under study, checked for fidelity by hostile review, and displayed with the file. Everything in H(s)H is geometry, and if the geometry isn't correct, then the math is uncoupled, unnecessary, or irrelevant. Same goes for basically all papers. If a statement makes a point about a geometric form (and...that means basically everything we do)... then what exactly it means has to be shown.  Math allows precision and fitting. But it's not the object. It's not the physical object, and it's not the theoretical object. The theoretical object is the geometry. If we have only the math, we have the handbook to the car. That's great, but it's only a description of a model, it's a pentary object. The quaternary object is a precise static diagram. The tertiary object is the precision dynamic geometry as a software model. The secondary object is a physical working orrery or hands-on demonstration. The primary object is observation. SAT is our K-T Boundary, as it were.

3. Study recursion and multi-agent/superorganismal organization with measurable error propagation and shared-memory interventions; avoid unearned claims of consciousness or ontology.
4. Review primary LLM cognition literature and internal RMS/FIE sources with citations and actual coverage.

items.snippet: [$github](app://connector_76869538009648d5b282a4bb21c3d157)  One non-negotiable: Nothing gets into Factory floor unless it has a precise geometric plot of the system under study, checked for fidelity by hostile review, and displayed with the file. Everything in H(s)H is geometry, and if the geometry isn't correct, then the math is uncoupled, unnecessary, or irrelevant. Same goes for basically all papers. If a statement makes a point about a geometric form (and...that means basically everything we do)... then what exactly it means has to be shown.  Math allows precision and fitting. But it's not the object. It's not the physical object, and it's not the theoretical object. The theoretical object is the geometry. If we have only the math, we have the handbook to the car. That's great, but it's only a description of a model, it's a pentary object. The quaternary object is a precise static diagram. The tertiary object is the precision dynamic geometry as a software model. The secondary object is a physical working orrery or hands-on demonstration. The primary object is observation. SAT is our K-T Boundary, as it were.

The Relativistic–Quantum Isomorphism asserts that General Relativity (GR) and Quantum Mechanics (QM) are not fundamentally separate theories, but two projection regimes of the same underlying 4D superhelical worldline dynamics. 	•	GR: Captures the low-frequency, global bending of worldlines. The curvature of spacetime, perceived as gravity, corresponds to the inertial resistance of a worldline constrained by the manifold geometry.
	•	QM: Captures the high-frequency, local vibrational modes of the same worldlines. Discrete energy levels (like the Hydrogen ladder) emerge from harmonic resonance of these modes within the curved manifold.

The isomorphism is a mathematical identity: the curvature patterns that define relativistic trajectories are directly related to the eigenvalue spectrum that defines quantum states.

⸻

2. Relativistic Side: Geometric Projection of GR

2.1 Manifold Constraints
	•	Worldlines $X(\lambda)$ are constrained to the hypersphere $S^3$ of radius $R$:
$$|X(\lambda)|^2 = R^2$$
	•	Without constraints, a worldline in $R^4$ would move linearly: $X’’ = 0$.
	•	Constraining to $S^3$ produces a geodesic equation via Lagrange multipliers on the action:
$$S = \int \frac{1}{2} |X’|^2 d\lambda + \Lambda(|X|^2 - R^2)$$
Variation yields:
$$X’’(\lambda) + \frac{|X’(\lambda)|^2}{R^2} X(\lambda) = 0$$

2.2 Physical Interpretation
	•	The term $|X’’|^2$ represents bending energy, analogous to curvature in GR.
	•	Radial acceleration in this equation corresponds to the relativistic potential: the worldline resists deviation from the manifold, producing an emergent gravitational effect.
	•	No external Schwarzschild metric is required: gravity is purely the inertial effect of worldline curvature.

	•	Quantum energy levels arise from harmonic vibrations of the same worldlines constrained to $S^3$.

$$\nabla^2_{S^3} f = -\lambda_l f, \quad \lambda_l = \frac{l(l+2)}{R^2}$$

	•	Bending energy term ($|H’’|^2$) → GR (curvature of worldlines).

	•	This links the low-frequency bending energy to high-frequency Laplacian stiffness.
	•	Both regimes are different frequency projections of the same underlying worldline geometry.

	•	$G$ is derived without empirical fitting: it is a geometric ratio between worldline scale ($\ell_f$), mass anchor ($m_0$), and topological overlap ($\Omega$):
$$G = c^2 \cdot \frac{\ell_f}{m_0} \cdot \Omega$$

	•	Numerically recovers $G \approx 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$ m³/kg·s², confirming that the same geometric structure governing quantum vibrations also dictates macroscopic gravity.
